chem_edx.4.0.summary: The **reactivity series** ranks metals by how vigorously they react, and Edexcel wants you to deduce that order from experiments: reactions with **water**, with **dilute acid** and **displacement reactions**. The deeper reason for the order is the **tendency of a metal to lose electrons and form its positive ion**. Displacement reactions are **redox** reactions: the more reactive metal is **oxidised** (loses electrons) and the ion of the less reactive metal is **reduced** (gains electrons).

core.h: The reactivity series you must learn
core.p: The Edexcel specification lists the metals in this order, most reactive first, with carbon and hydrogen included as non-metal reference points. Learn it exactly, because questions ask you to place carbon and hydrogen and to use them to predict extraction and reactions with acid.
bullets: Order (most to least reactive): **potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold**.
A common mnemonic: 'Please Send Cats, Monkeys And Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries Signed Gordon'.
Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc: metals below carbon can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon.
Hydrogen sits between iron and copper: metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to give hydrogen gas; copper, silver and gold do not.
The higher a metal is in the series, the **more easily it loses electrons** to form a positive ion, so the more reactive it is.
Gold is so unreactive that it is found **native** (uncombined) in the ground.

callouts.p: Carbon: between aluminium and zinc. Hydrogen: between iron and copper. These two are not metals but are used as reference points.

core.p: When metals react they **lose their outer shell electrons to form positive ions**. Reactivity depends on how easily this happens. Potassium has one outer electron that is lost very easily, so it reacts violently; gold holds on to its electrons strongly and hardly reacts at all.
bullets: Reactivity series = order of the **tendency of a metal to form its positive ion**.
Group 1 metals form 1+ ions (Na+, K+); Group 2 form 2+ ions (Mg2+, Ca2+); aluminium forms Al3+.
Iron commonly forms Fe2+ or Fe3+, zinc forms Zn2+, copper forms Cu2+, silver forms Ag+.
A more reactive metal will 'push' its electrons onto the ion of a less reactive metal: this is why displacement happens.
Higher-tier link: down a group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily, which is why potassium is more reactive than sodium.

callouts.p: A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, based on the tendency of each metal to lose electrons and form positive ions.

core.p: Only the most reactive metals react with cold water. They form a **metal hydroxide** (an alkali for Group 1) and **hydrogen gas**. Less reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc and iron react only with **steam**, forming a **metal oxide** and hydrogen.
bullets: General: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
2K(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H2(g)
Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g) (calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so the water goes cloudy).
With steam: metal + steam → metal oxide + hydrogen, for example Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g).
Observations to quote: **fizzing/effervescence**, metal **moves around**, metal **gets smaller and disappears**, sodium and potassium **melt**, potassium gives a **lilac flame**.
Universal indicator turns **purple/blue** because an alkaline hydroxide forms.

callouts.p: With cold water, metals form a hydroxide. With steam, metals form an oxide. Do not mix them up.

core.h: Reactions of metals with dilute acids
core.p: Metals above hydrogen react with **dilute hydrochloric acid** or **dilute sulfuric acid** to form a **salt and hydrogen**. The rate of bubbling, the temperature rise and how fast the metal disappears let you rank the metals.
bullets: General: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)
Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Copper, silver and gold are **below hydrogen**, so there is **no reaction** with dilute acids.
Hydrochloric acid gives **chlorides**; sulfuric acid gives **sulfates**.
Test for hydrogen: a **lighted splint** gives a **squeaky pop**.
Potassium, sodium (and calcium in strong acid) are too dangerous to add to acid in school.

callouts.p: In 'describe what you would see' questions, write bubbles/fizzing, metal gets smaller, solution gets warmer. 'Hydrogen is made' is not an observation.

core.h: Deducing an order of reactivity from experiments
core.p: Spec point 4.1 asks you to **deduce** an order of reactivity from results. You must make the comparison **fair**, then use evidence such as the rate of bubbling, the temperature rise or whether displacement happens.
bullets: Use the **same mass or same surface area** of each metal (for example, same size strips or same mass of powder).
Use the **same volume and concentration** of acid, and the same starting temperature.
Measure the **temperature rise** with a thermometer: a bigger rise in the same time means a more reactive metal (the reaction is exothermic).
Or **count bubbles** / collect hydrogen in a gas syringe over a fixed time: a faster rate means a more reactive metal.
Displacement grid: put each metal into solutions of salts of the other metals and record where a reaction happens. The metal that displaces the most others is the most reactive.
Repeat and calculate means to make results **repeatable**; avoid metals that react dangerously (K, Na, Ca with acid).

callouts.p: Count the ticks for each metal. Magnesium: 2 reactions, zinc: 1, copper: 0. So the order is magnesium > zinc > copper.

core.p: In a displacement reaction a **more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound** (usually a salt solution or a metal oxide). If the added metal is less reactive, nothing happens.
bullets: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Mg(s) + CuSO4(aq) → MgSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s): the solution turns blue and silver crystals form.
Cu(s) + ZnSO4(aq) → no reaction, because copper is less reactive than zinc.
Observations with copper sulfate: **blue colour fades** (copper ions used up), **brown/pink-orange solid** forms on the metal, the mixture **gets warmer**.
With metal oxides (heated): 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe (the thermite reaction).
The bigger the gap in the reactivity series, the more exothermic the displacement reaction, so the temperature rise can be used to rank metals.

callouts.p: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.

core.p: Edexcel defines oxidation and reduction in **two ways**: by **oxygen** and by **electrons**. Displacement reactions must be explained as redox reactions in terms of gain or loss of oxygen and loss or gain of electrons.
bullets: **Oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen** OR the **loss of electrons**.
**Reduction** is the **loss of oxygen** OR the **gain of electrons**.
Mnemonic **OIL RIG**: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Oxidation and reduction always happen **together**: electrons lost by one substance are gained by another, so the reaction is called **redox**.
Example (oxygen): 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe. Aluminium **gains oxygen** (oxidised); iron(III) oxide **loses oxygen** (reduced).
Example (electrons): in Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu, zinc **loses electrons** (oxidised) and copper ions **gain electrons** (reduced).

callouts.p: The gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons.
The loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons.
A reaction in which both oxidation and reduction occur.

core.h: Displacement as electron transfer: ionic and half equations
core.p: In solution, the sulfate (or nitrate) ions do not change. They are **spectator ions**. Removing them leaves an **ionic equation** that shows the real change: electrons transferring from the more reactive metal atom to the less reactive metal ion. Splitting this into **half equations** shows the oxidation and the reduction separately (Higher tier).
bullets: Full equation: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Oxidation half equation: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-
Reduction half equation: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu
Magnesium with copper ions: Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu
Copper with silver ions: Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag; the half equations are Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- and Ag+ + e- → Ag (twice).
The number of electrons lost in the oxidation half equation must equal the number gained in the reduction half equation.
The SO4 2- ions are spectators: they are in the solution at the start and the end, unchanged.

callouts.p: In a metal displacement reaction the MORE reactive metal atom is always oxidised (it becomes an ion) and the LESS reactive metal ion is always reduced (it becomes an atom).
Check half equations by adding the charges: Cu2+ + 2e- gives (+2) + (-2) = 0, which equals the charge on Cu.

core.p: A substance that causes another to be reduced is a **reducing agent**; it is itself oxidised. A substance that causes another to be oxidised is an **oxidising agent**; it is itself reduced. This language helps at grade 9 when explaining extraction and the thermite reaction.
bullets: In Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu, zinc is the **reducing agent** (it gives electrons to Cu2+).
Cu2+ is the **oxidising agent** (it takes electrons from zinc).
In the thermite reaction, aluminium is the reducing agent: it removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide.
More reactive metals are better reducing agents because they lose electrons more readily.

callouts.p: The reducing agent is oxidised. It sounds backwards, but the agent does to others the opposite of what happens to itself.

core.h: Using the reactivity series to predict reactions
core.p: Once you know the order you can predict whether a reaction will happen and what products form, even for metals you have not tested.
bullets: A metal **higher** in the series displaces a metal **lower** in the series from its compounds; never the reverse.
Silver nitrate + zinc: reaction, because zinc is above silver.
Magnesium sulfate + iron: no reaction, because iron is below magnesium.
A metal above hydrogen reacts with dilute acid; a metal below hydrogen does not.
An unknown metal X that displaces iron but not zinc must lie **between zinc and iron**.
Carbon can displace (reduce) metals below it from their oxides: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2 (links to extraction, covered in 4.4-4.7).

callouts.p: For 'explain why no reaction happens', write: copper is less reactive than zinc, so copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate (copper has a lower tendency to form positive ions).

core.p: Questions often describe a practical and ask you to improve it or explain a hazard. Know the control variables and safety points.
bullets: Wear **eye protection**; dilute acids are irritants.
Group 1 metals are stored **under oil** to stop them reacting with air and water; use only small pieces, behind a safety screen.
Use **fresh, cleaned** metal (rub with emery paper) to remove the oxide layer, which otherwise slows the reaction (aluminium especially).
Use an **insulated** container (polystyrene cup) when measuring temperature changes to reduce heat loss.
Keep the **particle size** the same, as powders react faster than strips because of greater surface area.
Aluminium often appears **less reactive than expected** because of its protective oxide layer.

callouts.p: If aluminium seems unreactive in an experiment, the reason is its thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide, not that it is low in the series.

analogy.p: Think of electrons as balls and metals as children. Potassium is a child who hates holding the ball and throws it away instantly; gold clings to it. In a displacement reaction a more 'throw-happy' child (zinc) passes its balls to a child who will accept them (Cu2+), so zinc ends up empty-handed (oxidised, Zn2+) and copper ends up holding them (reduced, Cu atom). A child who wants to keep their ball (copper) will not hand it to zinc ions, so no reaction. It breaks down because real electron transfer depends on energy changes, not choice, and 'throwing' happens to several electrons at once in a fixed ratio.

mistakes.w: Oxidation is gaining electrons.
mistakes.r: Oxidation is LOSS of electrons (or gain of oxygen); reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG).

mistakes.w: Copper displaces zinc from zinc sulfate.
mistakes.r: No reaction: copper is less reactive than zinc so cannot displace it.

mistakes.w: Sodium reacts with water to form sodium oxide and hydrogen.
mistakes.r: Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is given off (as an observation).
mistakes.r: Observations: fizzing/bubbles, metal gets smaller, solution gets warmer.

mistakes.w: In Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu, the copper is oxidised because it becomes copper metal.
mistakes.r: Cu2+ gains electrons so is reduced; zinc loses electrons so is oxidised.

mistakes.w: Writing the half equation as Cu2+ - 2e- → Cu.
mistakes.r: Electrons are added on the left in reduction: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.

mistakes.w: More reactive metals gain electrons more easily.
mistakes.r: More reactive metals LOSE electrons more easily to form positive ions.

mistakes.w: The sulfate ions are reduced in the displacement reaction.
mistakes.r: Sulfate ions are spectator ions and do not change.

mistakes.w: Copper reacts slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid.
mistakes.r: Copper is below hydrogen so does not react with dilute acids.

so copper cannot displace iron (from its compound)
exam.tip: Use the comparative word 'less reactive'.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the reaction between zinc and copper(II) sulfate is a redox reaction.
model: zinc atoms lose electrons, so zinc is oxidised
copper ions gain electrons, so copper ions are reduced
oxidation and reduction occur at the same time
exam.tip: Name which species loses and which gains.

exam.q: Aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe. Identify the substance oxidised and explain your answer in terms of oxygen.
model: aluminium
it gains oxygen
exam.tip: The oxygen definition is used for oxide reactions.

exam.q: Metal X displaces copper from copper sulfate but not zinc from zinc sulfate. X reacts with dilute acid. Suggest where X fits in the reactivity series.
model: below zinc
above copper (and above hydrogen), e.g. between zinc and hydrogen
exam.tip: Combine all three pieces of evidence.

exam.q: Describe how you could use temperature changes to find the order of reactivity of magnesium, zinc and iron using dilute hydrochloric acid.
model: measure the same volume and concentration of acid into an insulated cup
record the starting temperature
add the same mass of metal powder and stir
record the maximum temperature; bigger temperature rise = more reactive metal
exam.tip: Name the control variables and say how the results give the order.

exam.q: Explain the order of reactivity of potassium, magnesium, copper and gold, and describe evidence from their reactions with water and dilute acid that supports this order.
model: reactivity depends on the tendency of a metal to lose electrons and form positive ions
potassium forms its ion most easily, gold least easily
potassium reacts vigorously with cold water, fizzing, melting, lilac flame, forming potassium hydroxide and hydrogen
magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but vigorously with dilute acid, giving rapid bubbles of hydrogen
copper does not react with water or dilute acid because it is below hydrogen
gold does not react at all and is found native/uncombined
exam.tip: Six-markers need a linked chain: explanation plus evidence for each metal.

worked.q: Results of a displacement experiment: metal A displaces B and C; metal B displaces C only; metal C displaces nothing. Put A, B and C in order of reactivity.
steps: Count the number of displacements for each metal: A = 2, B = 1, C = 0.
The metal that displaces the most others is the most reactive.
So the order is A > B > C.
worked.ans: Most reactive A, then B, least reactive C.

worked.q: Copper is placed in silver nitrate solution. Write the full equation, the ionic equation and both half equations, and identify what is oxidised and reduced.
steps: Copper is above silver, so it displaces silver.
Full: Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s)
Nitrate ions are spectators. Ionic: Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag
Oxidation: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-
Reduction: Ag+ + e- → Ag (happens twice, so 2Ag+ + 2e- → 2Ag)
Copper loses electrons, so it is oxidised; silver ions gain electrons, so they are reduced.
worked.ans: Copper atoms are oxidised to Cu2+; Ag+ ions are reduced to silver atoms.

worked.q: In an experiment, 1 g of each metal powder was added to 25 cm3 of copper sulfate solution. Temperature rises: magnesium 18 °C, zinc 9 °C, iron 5 °C. Deduce the order and explain.
steps: Displacement reactions are exothermic.
The further apart the two metals are in the series, the more energy is released, so the bigger the temperature rise.
Magnesium gave the largest rise, then zinc, then iron.
worked.ans: Magnesium > zinc > iron: magnesium has the greatest tendency to form positive ions.

chem_edx.4.1.summary: Most metals are found in the Earth's crust combined with other elements in **ores**, so they must be **extracted by reduction** (removing oxygen). Very unreactive metals such as gold are found **uncombined** as the element. The method chosen depends on the metal's **position in the reactivity series** and on **cost**: metals below carbon (such as iron) are extracted by **heating with carbon**, while metals above carbon (such as aluminium) must be extracted by **electrolysis**, which is far more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity.

core.h: Ores and where metals come from
core.p: Metals are found in the **Earth's crust**. Most are reactive enough to have combined with oxygen, sulfur or other elements, forming compounds in rocks. An **ore** is a rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal economically worthwhile.
bullets: Most metals are extracted from **ores found in the Earth's crust**.
Ores usually contain **metal oxides** (or compounds that can be converted to oxides, such as sulfides or carbonates).
Iron ore: **haematite**, mainly iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.
Aluminium ore: **bauxite**, mainly aluminium oxide, Al2O3.
The ore is usually **mined**, then **concentrated** (unwanted rock removed) before extraction.
Whether an ore is worth mining depends on the **percentage of metal**, the **price of the metal** and the **cost of extraction**; this can change over time.

callouts.p: A rock or mineral that contains enough of a metal or metal compound to make it economical to extract the metal.

core.p: Metals at the very bottom of the reactivity series are so unreactive that they do not combine with oxygen or other elements. They are found in the ground as the **uncombined element** (native metal) and only need to be separated physically from rock.
bullets: **Gold** is found uncombined (nuggets, flakes in rivers).
Silver, and sometimes copper and platinum, can also be found native.
No chemical reduction is needed: the metal is separated physically, for example by panning or by chemical processes that dissolve the metal out.
Reason: these metals have a **very low tendency to form positive ions**, so they do not react with oxygen or water in the environment.

callouts.p: Reactive metals: in compounds within ores, must be extracted chemically. Very unreactive metals (gold): found as the uncombined element.

core.h: Oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen
core.p: Spec point 4.5 asks you to explain oxidation and reduction in terms of **oxygen**. Extracting a metal from its oxide means removing oxygen, which is reduction.
bullets: **Oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen** by a substance.
**Reduction** is the **loss of oxygen** from a substance.
Example: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2. Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen (reduced); carbon gains oxygen (oxidised).
Oxidation and reduction occur together: this is a **redox** reaction.
The substance that removes the oxygen (here carbon) is called the **reducing agent**.
Higher-tier link: in electrolysis, reduction is also seen as **gain of electrons** at the cathode.

head: Term
Oxygen definition
Example from extraction
rows: C gains O to form CO2
Fe2O3 loses O to form Fe

callouts.p: The gain of oxygen by a substance.
The loss of oxygen from a substance.

core.p: Because ores contain metal compounds (mostly oxides), getting the metal out always involves **reduction of the ore**. Spec point 4.6 is simply this recall statement, but you must be able to apply it to equations.
bullets: Extraction of metals involves **reduction of ores**.
In carbon reduction the ore **loses oxygen** to carbon.
In electrolysis the metal ions **gain electrons** at the cathode, which is also reduction.
Example: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2 (iron(III) oxide is reduced).
Example: 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2 (overall equation for electrolysis of aluminium oxide).

callouts.p: Write 'the iron oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen'. Saying 'iron is reduced' alone may not score unless you link it to loss of oxygen.

core.h: Choosing the method: reactivity series and cost
core.p: The method used to extract a metal depends on **where it is in the reactivity series compared with carbon**, and on the **cost** of the process. Carbon is cheap and can only remove oxygen from metals less reactive than itself.
bullets: Metals **below carbon** (zinc, iron, copper, lead, tin) can be extracted by **heating the oxide with carbon**. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen.

Metals **above carbon** (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) **cannot** be reduced by carbon, because carbon is less reactive. They must be extracted by **electrolysis** of a molten compound.
Heating with carbon is **cheaper**: carbon (coke) is cheap and abundant, and the process needs only heat.
Electrolysis is **expensive**: it needs **large amounts of electricity**, plus energy to **melt** the compound.
So electrolysis is used only when it is the only option: the more reactive the metal, the harder and more expensive it is to extract.
Very unreactive metals (gold) need no reduction at all.

callouts.p: Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals that are less reactive than carbon. More reactive metals need electrolysis.

core.p: Iron is below carbon in the reactivity series, so iron(III) oxide can be reduced by heating with carbon. In industry carbon is used as **coke**, and carbon monoxide formed from it does much of the reducing. Knowledge of the blast furnace itself is not required by Edexcel, but the chemistry is.
bullets: Word equation: iron(III) oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide.
Balanced: 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2
With carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2
Iron(III) oxide **loses oxygen**: it is **reduced**.
Carbon (or carbon monoxide) **gains oxygen**: it is **oxidised**; it is the **reducing agent**.
High temperatures are needed for a fast enough reaction, provided by burning some of the coke.
Other metals extracted this way: zinc (ZnO + C → Zn + CO) and copper (2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2).

callouts.p: 4 Fe on each side; 6 O on the left go into 3 CO2 on the right. Check every element after balancing.

core.p: Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide. Instead **molten** aluminium oxide is electrolysed. The ions must be free to move, which means the oxide must be melted or dissolved.
bullets: Ore: **bauxite**, purified to give **aluminium oxide**, Al2O3.
Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C), so it is **dissolved in molten cryolite** to **lower the operating temperature** (to about 950 °C), saving energy and cost.
Electrodes are made of **graphite (carbon)**.
At the **cathode (negative)**: aluminium ions gain electrons: **Al3+ + 3e- → Al**. This is **reduction**. Molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.
At the **anode (positive)**: oxide ions lose electrons: **2O2- → O2 + 4e-**. This is **oxidation**.
The oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form **carbon dioxide**, so the **anodes burn away and must be replaced** regularly.
Overall: 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2.

callouts.p: Dissolving aluminium oxide in molten cryolite lowers the temperature needed, so less energy is used and the process is cheaper.
Solid aluminium oxide does not conduct: its ions are fixed in a lattice. It must be molten (or dissolved) so ions can move to the electrodes.

core.p: Electrolysis is used for reactive metals only because there is no cheaper alternative. Its costs come from energy, materials and maintenance.
bullets: **Large amounts of electricity** are needed to pass a high current through the cell.
**Energy to melt** the compound and keep it molten (even with cryolite, about 950 °C).
Carbon **anodes must be replaced** frequently because they react with oxygen.
Producing and purifying the aluminium oxide from bauxite adds cost.
Aluminium plants are often built near **cheap electricity**, such as hydroelectric power stations.
Environmental cost: carbon dioxide from the anodes, and CO2 from power stations if fossil fuels generate the electricity.

callouts.p: Always mention 'large amounts of electricity' (energy) when asked why aluminium costs more to extract than iron.

core.p: Electrolysis also shows reduction and oxidation, but in terms of **electrons**. This links extraction back to the OIL RIG definitions from the reactivity series.
bullets: Cathode: positive metal ions **gain electrons**: reduction (Al3+ + 3e- → Al).
Anode: negative ions **lose electrons**: oxidation (2O2- → O2 + 4e-).
Balanced for the whole cell: 4Al3+ + 12e- → 4Al and 6O2- → 3O2 + 12e-.
The electrons lost at the anode equal the electrons gained at the cathode.
Anode reaction with carbon: C + O2 → CO2 (carbon is oxidised).

callouts.p: Cathode = reduction (both consonants); Anode = oxidation (both vowels).

core.h: Applying the ideas to unfamiliar metals
core.p: Exam questions often give data for a metal you have not studied (for example titanium, tin or chromium) and ask you to suggest a method or evaluate cost.
bullets: If the metal is **less reactive than carbon**, suggest heating its oxide with carbon.
If it is **more reactive than carbon**, suggest electrolysis of the molten compound.

A metal can also be extracted by **displacement** with a more reactive metal (for example titanium chloride reduced by sodium or magnesium), but this is expensive because the reactive metal itself was made by electrolysis.
If carbon would form unwanted compounds with the metal (such as carbides), another method may be chosen even if carbon is reactive enough.
Low-grade ores may use biological methods instead (covered in 4.8).

callouts.p: When a question gives a reactivity series including an unfamiliar metal, compare it with carbon before choosing a method, and quote the comparison in your answer.

core.h: Linking ideas: reactivity and difficulty of extraction
core.p: The more reactive a metal is, the more strongly it is held in its compounds, so the more energy is needed to extract it. This explains history as well as cost.
bullets: Gold and silver were used thousands of years ago because they occur native.
Copper and iron were extracted early using charcoal (carbon) fires.
Aluminium, despite being the most abundant metal in the crust, was only produced in large amounts after electrolysis became practical in the late 1800s.
Reactive metals form very stable compounds: a large energy input is needed to reverse the formation reaction.
So: **more reactive metal → harder to extract → more expensive method**.

callouts.p: Extraction method is decided by reactivity (can carbon reduce it?) and then by cost (choose the cheapest method that works).

analogy.p: A metal in an ore is a hostage held by oxygen. To free it you need a rescuer that oxygen likes more. Carbon is a cheap rescuer that oxygen prefers to iron or copper, so oxygen lets go of them and grabs carbon instead (forming CO2). For aluminium, oxygen is more attached to the aluminium than it would be to carbon, so carbon cannot tempt it away: you must pay for an expensive 'force' (electricity) to pull them apart. The analogy breaks down because atoms make no choices; what really decides it is relative reactivity and energy changes, and electrolysis works by moving electrons, not by force on oxygen.

terms.d: A rock or mineral containing enough of a metal compound for extraction of the metal to be economical.
A metal found in the Earth as the element, not in a compound, because it is very unreactive, for example gold.
Gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons).
Loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons).
Obtaining a metal from its ore, which involves reduction of the metal compound.
A substance that removes oxygen from (or gives electrons to) another substance, for example carbon.
An ore of iron containing iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.
An ore of aluminium containing aluminium oxide, Al2O3.
The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in solution, using electricity.
A molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity because its ions can move.
The negative electrode, where positive ions gain electrons (reduction).
The positive electrode, where negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
An aluminium compound in which aluminium oxide is dissolved to lower the temperature needed for electrolysis.
A form of almost pure carbon made from coal, used as the reducing agent and fuel in iron extraction.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time.

exam.q: State what is meant by an ore.
model: rock/mineral containing enough metal (compound) to make extraction economical/worthwhile
exam.tip: The word 'economical' or 'worthwhile' is needed.

exam.q: Explain why gold is found uncombined in the Earth's crust.
model: gold is very unreactive / at the bottom of the reactivity series
so it does not react with oxygen or other elements
exam.tip: Link reactivity to not forming compounds.

exam.q: State what is meant by reduction in terms of oxygen.
model: loss of oxygen
exam.tip: Do not confuse with oxidation.

exam.q: Iron(III) oxide is heated with carbon. Balance: Fe2O3 + C → Fe + CO2
model: 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2
exam.tip: Balance Fe and O, then check carbon.

exam.q: In the reaction Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, identify the substance that is reduced and give a reason.
model: iron(III) oxide / Fe2O3
it loses oxygen
exam.tip: Name the compound, not just 'iron'.

exam.q: Explain why iron can be extracted by heating with carbon but aluminium cannot.
model: iron is less reactive than carbon
so carbon can remove oxygen from iron oxide / reduce it
aluminium is more reactive than carbon so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
exam.tip: Compare each metal with carbon.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the extraction of aluminium is expensive.
model: large amounts of electricity needed
high temperature / energy to melt the electrolyte
anodes need replacing (any two)
exam.tip: Electricity is the main answer.

exam.q: Explain why aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite.
model: lowers the melting point / operating temperature
so less energy needed / reduces cost
exam.tip: Give the effect and the reason it matters.

exam.q: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode in the extraction of aluminium.
model: Al3+ + 3e- → Al
exam.tip: Three electrons for a 3+ ion.

exam.q: Explain why the positive electrodes must be replaced regularly in aluminium extraction.
model: oxygen is formed at the anode
it reacts with the carbon anode to form carbon dioxide, so the anode wears away
exam.tip: Include the product, carbon dioxide.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of heating with carbon and electrolysis for extracting metals, explaining how the method chosen depends on the position of the metal in the reactivity series and on cost.
model: metals are extracted by reduction of their ores
metals less reactive than carbon, e.g. iron, are reduced by heating with carbon
carbon gains oxygen / is oxidised; the metal oxide loses oxygen / is reduced
this is relatively cheap as carbon is cheap and only heat is needed
metals more reactive than carbon, e.g. aluminium, cannot be reduced by carbon so electrolysis of the molten compound is used
electrolysis is expensive because large amounts of electricity and energy to melt the compound are needed, so the cheapest method that works is chosen
exam.tip: Cover both methods, an example of each, and an explicit link to cost.

worked.q: Tin is between iron and copper in the reactivity series. Suggest how tin could be extracted from tin(IV) oxide, SnO2, and write a balanced equation.
steps: Tin is below iron, so it is below carbon.
Carbon is more reactive, so carbon can remove oxygen from tin oxide.
Heat tin(IV) oxide with carbon.
SnO2 + C → Sn + CO2 (1 Sn, 2 O, 1 C on each side).
Tin oxide is reduced (loses oxygen); carbon is oxidised.
worked.ans: Heat SnO2 with carbon: SnO2 + C → Sn + CO2.

worked.q: Write balanced half equations for both electrodes in the electrolysis of aluminium oxide, and show they combine to give the overall equation 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2.
steps: Cathode: Al3+ + 3e- → Al
Anode: 2O2- → O2 + 4e-
Lowest common multiple of 3 and 4 is 12 electrons.
Cathode x4: 4Al3+ + 12e- → 4Al
Anode x3: 6O2- → 3O2 + 12e-
Add and cancel electrons: 4Al3+ + 6O2- → 4Al + 3O2, which is 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2.
worked.ans: Cathode Al3+ + 3e- → Al; anode 2O2- → O2 + 4e-; overall 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of iron that could be obtained from 320 tonnes of Fe2O3. (Ar Fe = 56, O = 16)
steps: Mass of iron in one formula unit = 112
Fraction of iron = 112 / 160 = 0.7
Mass of iron = 0.7 x 320 = 224 tonnes
worked.ans: 224 tonnes of iron.

chem_edx.4.2.summary: High-grade metal ores, especially copper ores, are running out, so biological methods are used to extract metals from **low-grade ores** and waste. In **bacterial extraction (bioleaching)** bacteria break down ores to produce a solution called a **leachate** containing metal ions. In **phytoextraction** plants absorb metal compounds through their roots, are harvested and **burned**, and the metal is extracted from the **ash**. Edexcel asks you to **evaluate** these methods: they use less energy and cause less damage than traditional mining and smelting, but they are **slow**.

core.h: Why we need alternative extraction methods
core.p: Traditional extraction involves mining large amounts of ore and then smelting or electrolysis. The best (**high-grade**) ores of metals such as copper are being used up, leaving **low-grade ores** with only a small percentage of metal. Extracting metal from these by traditional methods would mean digging and processing huge amounts of rock for very little metal.
bullets: Metal ores are a **finite** (non-renewable) resource.
**Low-grade ores** contain a small proportion of metal compound, so traditional extraction would be **uneconomical** and very damaging.
Mining produces large **scars on the landscape**, noise, dust and huge **waste heaps (spoil)**.
Smelting uses large amounts of **energy** (usually from fossil fuels), releasing **carbon dioxide**; smelting sulfide ores also releases **sulfur dioxide**, causing **acid rain**.
Biological methods can use low-grade ores, **mine waste** and **contaminated land**.
Edexcel names two methods: **bacterial extraction** and **phytoextraction**.

callouts.p: An ore that contains only a small percentage of the metal or metal compound.

core.p: Certain **bacteria** can obtain energy from the chemical bonds in metal sulfide ores. As they feed, they break the ore down and **release the metal ions into solution**. The resulting solution is called a **leachate**.
bullets: Bacteria are added to low-grade ore (often heaped up and sprayed with dilute acid and water).
The bacteria **break down the ore**, for example copper sulfide, releasing **copper(II) ions, Cu2+**, into solution.
The solution containing the metal ions is the **leachate**; it drains to the bottom of the heap and is collected.
The leachate contains a **higher concentration of metal ions** than the original rock had metal, so the metal is now easier to extract.
The metal is then obtained from the leachate by **displacement** with scrap iron, or by **electrolysis**.
The process happens at **normal temperatures**, so little energy is needed for heating.

callouts.p: Using bacteria to break down a metal ore, producing a leachate solution that contains metal ions.
The solution produced by bioleaching, which contains metal ions.

core.p: The leachate is a solution of a copper compound (such as copper sulfate). Two methods recover the copper; both link back to ideas from the reactivity series and electrolysis.
bullets: **Displacement with scrap iron**: iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution.
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Ionic: Fe + Cu2+ → Fe2+ + Cu. Iron is oxidised; copper ions are reduced.
Scrap iron is **cheap**, which keeps costs down, and it recycles waste metal.
**Electrolysis** of the copper solution: copper ions gain electrons at the cathode, Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu, giving very pure copper.
Electrolysis needs electricity, so it is more expensive than displacement but gives purer copper.

callouts.p: Whether by scrap iron or electrolysis, copper ions gain electrons to become copper atoms: this is reduction.

core.p: Phytoextraction uses **plants** to concentrate metals. Some plants absorb metal compounds from the soil through their roots and store them in their **shoots and leaves**. Over time, the metal becomes concentrated in the plant tissue.
bullets: Plants are **grown on soil** containing low-grade ore, mine waste or contaminated land.
The plants **absorb metal compounds/ions through their roots** and concentrate them in their **shoots and leaves**.
The plants are **harvested**.
The plants are **burned**, leaving **ash** that contains a **high concentration of metal compounds**.
The metal is extracted from the ash, for example by dissolving it in acid to form a solution, then using **displacement** or **electrolysis**.
Energy released by burning the plants can sometimes be used to generate electricity.

callouts.p: Using plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil; the plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is extracted from the ash.

core.p: When evaluating, you must give **both advantages and disadvantages** and reach a **conclusion**. The main advantages come from avoiding large-scale mining and high-temperature smelting.
bullets: They can extract metals from **low-grade ores** and **mine waste** that would be uneconomical to process traditionally.
They help conserve the limited supplies of **high-grade ores**.
**Less energy** is needed: no high-temperature furnaces, so fewer fossil fuels burned and **less carbon dioxide** released.
**No sulfur dioxide** from roasting sulfide ores, so less acid rain.
**Less damage to the landscape**: less digging, transporting and dumping of waste rock.
Phytoextraction can **clean up contaminated land** (for example soil polluted with heavy metals) while recovering metal.
Phytoextraction plants can be burned to release energy; bacteria and plants are **cheap** to grow.

callouts.p: 'Better for the environment' scores nothing on its own. Say WHY: less energy used so less CO2, no SO2 released, less landscape destroyed by mining.

core.p: The big drawback is **speed**. Both methods take much longer than traditional extraction, and they produce only small amounts of metal.
bullets: Both processes are **very slow**: bioleaching can take months or years; plants take time to grow and need several harvests.
They produce **relatively small amounts** of metal, so cannot meet all demand alone.
Bioleaching produces **toxic substances**, including **sulfuric acid**, in the leachate; if it leaks it can **pollute groundwater**, rivers and soil.
Phytoextraction depends on **weather and growing seasons**, and needs large areas of land.
Burning plants releases carbon dioxide (although the plants absorbed CO2 when growing).
Further processing (displacement or electrolysis) is still needed to get the pure metal.

callouts.p: Bioleaching leachate is acidic and can contain toxic metal ions. Biological methods reduce some environmental impacts, not all.

core.p: A comparison table is the easiest way to organise an evaluation answer. Exam questions often give a table of data (time, energy, yield, cost) and ask you to use it.
bullets: Traditional: fast, large-scale, but high energy, high CO2/SO2, and needs high-grade ore.
Bioleaching: slow, low energy, uses low-grade ore, risk of toxic leachate.
Phytoextraction: slowest, low energy, cleans land, needs space and good growing conditions.
Always end an evaluation with a **justified conclusion**: for example, biological methods are best for low-grade ores and waste, while traditional methods are still needed for large-scale supply.

callouts.p: Bacteria produce a LEACHATE (solution of metal ions). Plants produce ASH (after burning). Both still need displacement or electrolysis to get the metal.

core.p: You are not expected to know the detailed biochemistry, but understanding the idea helps you explain why it works.
bullets: Bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus species obtain energy by **oxidising** sulfide (and iron(II)) in the ore.
This releases metal ions, such as Cu2+, into the acidic solution and produces sulfuric acid.
The bacteria work best in **acidic, warm, moist** conditions, so the ore heap is sprayed with dilute sulfuric acid and water.
Higher temperature speeds up the bacteria (up to a limit), but heaps still take months to process.
The process is a biological version of oxidising sulfide ores without heating them.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: 'bacteria break down the ore', 'produce a leachate', 'leachate contains metal ions/copper ions'.

core.p: Plants take in dissolved mineral ions through their roots as part of normal nutrition. Some species, called **hyperaccumulators**, take up unusually large amounts of particular metals and tolerate them.
bullets: Metal ions dissolved in soil water are absorbed by the **roots** and transported to shoots and leaves.
Concentrations in the plant can be far higher than in the soil.
Burning removes the carbon-based plant material as CO2 and water, so the metal compounds are **concentrated in the ash**.
The ash can be treated with acid to make a metal salt solution, then electrolysed or treated with scrap iron.
Used for copper and nickel, and for removing metals such as lead or zinc from contaminated soil.

callouts.p: Burning removes most of the plant mass, leaving a small amount of ash with a high concentration of metal compounds.

core.p: Spec point 4.8 uses the command word **evaluate**. This means: give advantages, give disadvantages, and then make a **judgement** supported by reasons. Six-mark questions are marked by levels, so a clear structure matters.
bullets: Step 1: describe briefly how the method works (bacteria → leachate; plants → ash).
Step 2: give at least two **advantages** with reasons (low-grade ores, less energy, less CO2/SO2, less landscape damage).
Step 3: give at least two **disadvantages** with reasons (slow, small yields, toxic leachate, land and weather).
Step 4: reach a **conclusion** that weighs the points, for example: useful as high-grade ores run out, but too slow to replace traditional methods completely.
Use data from the question if it is given (time, energy, percentage of metal).

callouts.p: Top-band answers link each point to a reason and finish with a justified judgement. Lists of points with no conclusion stay in the middle band.

core.h: Links to the rest of the topic
core.p: Biological methods connect to several other spec points, which examiners like to combine in longer questions.
bullets: Reactivity series (4.1-4.3): scrap iron displaces copper because iron is more reactive.
Extraction by reduction (4.4-4.7): getting copper from leachate or ash is still a reduction.
Recycling (4.10): like recycling, biological methods help conserve finite ores.
Life-cycle assessment (4.11-4.12): biological methods reduce the impact of the raw-material extraction stage.

callouts.p: Biological methods make it possible to extract metals from sources too poor for traditional methods, at a lower environmental cost but much more slowly.

analogy.p: Imagine a field with a few coins scattered through tonnes of soil. Digging up and sieving the whole field (traditional mining) is costly and wrecks the field. Instead you could hire tiny workers who slowly pick the coins out and drop them into a bucket (bacteria making a leachate), or plant sunflowers whose roots suck up the coins into their heads, which you then burn to leave a pile of coins in the ash (phytoextraction). Both are gentle but slow. The analogy breaks down because metals are taken up as dissolved ions, not solid lumps, and you still need chemistry (displacement or electrolysis) to turn the ions into metal.

An ore containing a large percentage of the metal or its compound.

chem_edx.4.3.summary: A metal's position in the reactivity series tells you how easily it is **oxidised**. Metals near the top (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium) react readily with oxygen and water because their atoms **lose electrons easily** to form positive ions, so they have **low resistance to oxidation**. Metals near the bottom (copper, silver, gold) lose electrons only with difficulty, so they **resist oxidation and corrosion** and the least reactive, such as gold, are even found uncombined in the Earth's crust. Aluminium is the classic exception that seems unreactive only because a **protective oxide layer** forms on its surface.

core.p: At GCSE you need two definitions of oxidation. The simpler one is about oxygen; the Higher tier one is about electrons. Both describe the same change when a metal reacts with oxygen to form a metal oxide.
bullets: **Oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen** by a substance, e.g. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (magnesium gains oxygen).
**Reduction** is the **loss of oxygen**, e.g. CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O (copper oxide loses oxygen).
Higher tier: **oxidation is loss of electrons**, **reduction is gain of electrons** (remember **OIL RIG**).
When a metal is oxidised its atoms become **positive ions (cations)**, e.g. Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-.
Oxidation and reduction always happen together in a **redox** reaction: in 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, magnesium is oxidised and oxygen is reduced (each O atom gains 2 electrons to form O2-).

callouts.p: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen, or (Higher) the loss of electrons.
Reduction is the loss of oxygen, or (Higher) the gain of electrons.

core.p: The reactivity series lists metals in order of how vigorously they react, for example with water, dilute acids and oxygen. Edexcel uses this order, with carbon and hydrogen included as non-metal reference points.
bullets: Order (most to least reactive): **potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold**.
A common mnemonic: Please Send Cats, Monkeys And Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries Signed Gordon.
Reactivity depends on the metal's **tendency to form positive ions** - how readily its atoms give away their outer electrons.
The higher the metal, the **more easily it is oxidised** and the **less resistant** it is to oxidation.
The lower the metal, the **more resistant to oxidation** it is, and the more stable the metal is compared with its compounds.

callouts.p: Higher in the reactivity series = oxidised more easily = lower resistance to oxidation. Lower in the series = greater resistance to oxidation.

core.h: Why position links to resistance to oxidation (electron explanation)
core.p: This is the grade 9 reasoning examiners want. When a metal is oxidised, its atoms lose their outer electrons to form positive ions. A metal high in the series loses those electrons very easily, so it reacts readily with oxygen; a metal low in the series holds on to its electrons more strongly, so it resists oxidation.
bullets: Metal atoms react by **losing outer-shell electrons** to become positive ions.
The **more easily** a metal atom loses electrons, the **more reactive** it is and the **more easily it is oxidised**.
Potassium loses its single outer electron very easily, so it is oxidised almost instantly in air and must be stored under oil.
Gold loses electrons with great difficulty, so it **does not react with oxygen** even when heated and stays shiny for thousands of years.
So the reactivity series is effectively a list of metals in order of their **tendency to form cations**, which is the same as their tendency to be oxidised.

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions about reactivity, Higher-tier marks usually require a statement such as 'magnesium atoms lose electrons more easily than copper atoms'. Saying only 'magnesium is more reactive' just repeats the question.

core.p: Most metals react with oxygen to form a metal oxide: metal + oxygen → metal oxide. How fast and how vigorously this happens follows the reactivity series, which is direct evidence that resistance to oxidation increases down the series.
bullets: Potassium and sodium: tarnish **within seconds** when cut, burn vigorously when heated. 4Na + O2 → 2Na2O.
Calcium and magnesium: magnesium ribbon burns with a **bright white flame** to form white magnesium oxide. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.
Zinc and iron: react slowly at room temperature; iron filings sparkle when sprinkled in a flame. Iron rusts in the presence of **water and oxygen**.
Copper: does not burn, but forms a **black layer of copper(II) oxide** when heated. 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO.
Silver: does not react with oxygen on heating in air (it tarnishes slowly at room temperature mainly due to sulfur compounds, not oxygen).
Gold: **no reaction at all**, even when strongly heated.

core.h: Metals found native in the Earth's crust
core.p: Because the least reactive metals are so resistant to oxidation, they do not combine with oxygen or other elements in the ground. They can be found as the uncombined element, which is called being found native.
bullets: **Gold** (and platinum) are found **native** - as nuggets or flakes of the pure metal.
Silver and copper are sometimes found native, but are usually found combined in ores.
Most metals above copper are only found **combined** as compounds (often oxides) in **ores**, because they react with oxygen and other substances in the environment.
Native metals need only to be **separated physically** from the rock; they do not need a chemical reduction step.
This explains history: gold and copper were among the first metals used by humans, while reactive metals such as potassium and aluminium were isolated only after electrolysis was developed.

callouts.p: A metal found in the Earth's crust as the uncombined element, because it is so unreactive.

core.h: Resistance to oxidation and ease of extraction
core.p: Resistance to oxidation is the reverse of how hard a metal is to extract. A metal that is easily oxidised forms a very stable oxide, which is hard to reduce back to the metal.
bullets: Metals **high** in the series form **stable compounds**: a lot of energy is needed to reduce them, so they are extracted by **electrolysis**.
Metals **below carbon** can be extracted by **reduction with carbon**, because carbon is more reactive and removes the oxygen.
Metals at the **bottom** (gold) need no reduction at all as they are already found native.
So: easily oxidised metal ↔ oxide hard to reduce; oxidation-resistant metal ↔ compounds easily reduced or not formed at all.

callouts.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to link a metal's reactivity, its resistance to oxidation, how it is found and how it is extracted. Practise writing this as one chain of reasoning.

core.p: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, above zinc and iron, yet aluminium window frames and drinks cans do not seem to corrode. This is because aluminium reacts with oxygen at once to form a very thin layer of aluminium oxide that protects it.
bullets: 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3 happens instantly on any fresh aluminium surface.
The **aluminium oxide layer** is thin, tough, **unreactive** and **sticks firmly** to the metal.
It acts as a **barrier**, stopping oxygen and water reaching the aluminium underneath, so further oxidation stops.
Aluminium is still a reactive metal: if the oxide layer is removed (e.g. by scratching under mercury salts or using acid), it reacts much faster.
This is why aluminium can **appear less reactive** than its position suggests, for example reacting slowly with dilute acid at first.

callouts.t: Do not say aluminium is unreactive
callouts.p: Aluminium resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer, not because it is low in the reactivity series.

core.p: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal by reaction with substances in its surroundings, mainly oxygen and water. It is an oxidation reaction, so the more reactive a metal, the faster it tends to corrode unless it is protected.
bullets: **Corrosion** = oxidation of a metal surface by its environment.
**Rusting** is the corrosion of **iron (or steel)** only; it needs **both water and oxygen**. Iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust).
Rust is **flaky and porous**, so unlike aluminium oxide it does not protect the iron below.
Gold, platinum and (to a large extent) copper and silver corrode very little because they are low in the series.
Because corrosion is oxidation, a **more reactive metal** in contact with iron (such as zinc) will be oxidised **instead** of the iron - the basis of sacrificial protection.

callouts.p: The oxidation of a metal by reaction with substances such as oxygen and water in its environment.

core.p: Engineers and jewellers choose metals partly for their resistance to oxidation. A metal low in the series keeps its appearance and properties for a long time.
bullets: **Gold**: jewellery and coins stay shiny; used for **electrical contacts** in electronics because no oxide layer forms to block the current.
**Copper**: water pipes and wiring; resists corrosion and does not react with water.
**Silver**: jewellery, cutlery, mirrors; resists oxidation but tarnishes slowly.
**Aluminium**: aircraft, window frames, cans; light and protected by its oxide layer.
**Iron/steel** must be **protected** (painting, oiling, galvanising with zinc) because it is easily oxidised to rust.

core.h: Displacement as evidence of the same order
core.p: Displacement reactions confirm the order of the reactivity series and show the electron link. A more reactive metal is more easily oxidised, so it gives electrons to the ions of a less reactive metal.
bullets: Zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper: zinc is **oxidised** (Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-), copper ions are **reduced** (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu).
The metal that is **more easily oxidised** always ends up as ions in solution.
Copper does **not** displace zinc, because copper is more resistant to oxidation than zinc.
Similarly, magnesium heated with copper oxide forms magnesium oxide and copper: the oxygen goes to the metal that is more easily oxidised.

core.h: Ordering unknown metals from oxidation evidence
core.p: Exam questions often give observations and ask you to place metals in order. Look for the speed and vigour of reaction with oxygen, water or acid, and for whether one metal displaces another.
bullets: Faster tarnishing in air or brighter burning = **higher** in the series = **less resistant** to oxidation.
No change on heating = very **low** in the series = **highly resistant**.
A metal that displaces another from its compound is **higher** in the series.
Always give a **reason** using the evidence and, for Higher, link to losing electrons to form positive ions.
Watch out for aluminium-type results: a reactive metal with a protective oxide may react slowly at first.

callouts.p: When comparing metals, use the same mass and surface area (e.g. same size pieces or same powder), the same heating or the same volume and concentration of acid.

core.h: Higher tier: half equations for oxidation
core.p: You may need to write half equations showing metals being oxidised. Electrons appear on the right-hand side because they are lost.
bullets: Na → Na+ + e-
Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-
Al → Al3+ + 3e-
Fe → Fe2+ + 2e- (or Fe → Fe3+ + 3e-)
The charges must balance: the total charge on each side is zero.
At the bottom of the series, gold atoms do not readily form Au+ or Au3+ ions, which is why gold resists oxidation.

callouts.p: For oxidation, write electrons as products (lost). Writing Mg + 2e- → Mg2+ is wrong: it neither balances the charge nor shows electron loss.

analogy.t: Metals holding on to pocket money
analogy.p: Think of each metal atom holding its outer electrons like pocket money. Potassium and sodium are big spenders - they hand over their electrons to oxygen the moment it asks, so they are oxidised at once. Gold is a miser who never gives any away, so it stays unchanged for centuries. Aluminium is a spender who has locked the money in a tough safe (the oxide layer), so it looks like a saver. Where it breaks down: atoms do not choose to give away electrons, and the 'ease' depends on energy changes for the whole reaction, not just one atom; also electrons are not spent and gone - they are transferred to the oxygen, which is reduced.

exam.q: State what is meant by oxidation in terms of oxygen.
model: Gain of oxygen (by a substance).
exam.tip: For 1 mark, a short precise definition is enough.

exam.q: Gold is found as the uncombined element in the Earth's crust. Explain why.
model: Gold is very unreactive / very low in the reactivity series.
So it does not react with oxygen (or other elements) / it is resistant to oxidation.
exam.tip: Give both the fact (low reactivity) and its consequence (does not combine with other elements).

exam.q: Magnesium is higher in the reactivity series than copper. Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium is oxidised more easily than copper.
model: Magnesium atoms lose (outer) electrons more easily than copper atoms.
So magnesium forms positive ions more readily.
exam.tip: Higher tier: you must mention losing electrons to form positive ions.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
model: Correct formulae: Mg, O2 and MgO.
Balanced: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.
exam.tip: Oxygen is diatomic (O2), so you need 2Mg and 2MgO.

exam.q: Write the half equation for the oxidation of aluminium atoms to aluminium ions.
model: Al → Al3+ + 3e-
exam.tip: Aluminium is in group 3, so it loses 3 electrons.

exam.q: Aluminium is above iron in the reactivity series, but aluminium objects corrode much less than iron objects. Explain why.
model: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a (thin) layer of aluminium oxide.
The aluminium oxide layer is unreactive / sticks to the surface / is not porous.
It stops oxygen (and water) reaching the aluminium so it prevents further oxidation (whereas rust flakes off).
exam.tip: The key word examiners look for is 'layer' (or 'coating') of aluminium oxide.

exam.q: A student heats samples of copper, gold and magnesium in air. Predict what is observed for each metal and explain the order.
model: Magnesium burns with a bright white flame, forming a white solid.
Copper forms a black coating (copper oxide) but does not burn.
Gold shows no change.
Order shows magnesium is most easily oxidised, gold most resistant, because reactivity / ease of losing electrons decreases from Mg to Cu to Au.
exam.tip: Match each observation to a metal, then give the reason linked to the reactivity series.

exam.q: When copper is heated in air the mass of the copper increases. Explain why.
model: Copper reacts with oxygen from the air.
Copper oxide forms, so the mass of oxygen added increases the mass.
exam.tip: Do not say mass is 'created'; mass is conserved but oxygen joins from the air.

exam.q: Explain which substance is oxidised and which is reduced when magnesium burns in oxygen, in terms of electrons.
model: Magnesium is oxidised.
Because magnesium atoms lose electrons (to form Mg2+).
Oxygen is reduced because oxygen atoms gain electrons (to form O2-).
exam.tip: State both species and say which gains and which loses electrons.

exam.q: Explain how the position of a metal in the reactivity series is related to its resistance to oxidation, how it is found in the Earth's crust and how it is extracted. Use examples in your answer.
model: Metals higher in the reactivity series lose electrons more easily / form positive ions more readily.
So they are oxidised more easily / have low resistance to oxidation.
They are found combined in compounds (ores), often as oxides, e.g. aluminium oxide in bauxite.
Their compounds are very stable so reactive metals (above carbon) are extracted by electrolysis, e.g. aluminium.
Metals below carbon, e.g. iron, are extracted by reduction with carbon.
Very unreactive metals, e.g. gold, resist oxidation so are found native and need no chemical reduction.
exam.tip: Level-marked: build a logical chain from reactivity to oxidation to occurrence to extraction, with named examples at each step.

worked.q: 2.4 g of magnesium is burned completely in air and forms 4.0 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted and explain why the mass increased.
steps: Mass of oxygen = mass of oxide - mass of metal.
The magnesium has been oxidised: it gained oxygen from the air (2Mg + O2 → 2MgO).
Mass is conserved overall; the extra mass is the oxygen that combined with the magnesium.
worked.ans: 1.6 g of oxygen reacted; the mass increased because oxygen from the air combined with the magnesium.

worked.q: Metals W, X and Y are tested. W tarnishes immediately when cut. X forms a black coating when heated but does not burn. Y does not change when heated. W displaces X from a solution of X sulfate. Place the metals in order of resistance to oxidation, least resistant first, and suggest identities.
steps: W tarnishes instantly, so it is very reactive and oxidised most easily - least resistant.
X reacts slowly with oxygen only when heated, so it is in the middle.
Y shows no reaction with oxygen, so it is the most resistant.
W displacing X confirms W is above X in the reactivity series.
Possible identities: W = sodium, X = copper, Y = gold.
worked.ans: Least to most resistant: W, X, Y (for example sodium, copper, gold).

worked.q: Zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Use the idea of resistance to oxidation to explain what happens and write the half equations (Higher).
steps: Zinc is higher in the reactivity series than copper, so zinc is less resistant to oxidation.
Zinc atoms lose electrons: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- (oxidation).
Copper ions gain these electrons: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (reduction).
Observations: brown copper forms, blue colour of solution fades, zinc gets smaller.
Overall: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.
worked.ans: Zinc is oxidised and displaces copper, because zinc atoms lose electrons more easily than copper atoms.

chem_edx.4.4.summary: Metals are extracted from **ores**, which are **finite resources** that will eventually run out. **Recycling** metals means collecting used metal items, sorting them and melting them down to make new products. Edexcel wants you to **evaluate** recycling: it **conserves raw materials**, usually **saves energy**, reduces mining damage, CO2 emissions and landfill, and can be **cheaper** than extraction - but collection, transport and sorting cost money and energy, so whether recycling is worthwhile depends on the metal and the situation.

core.h: Why metals need to be conserved
core.p: Metal ores are found in the Earth's crust in limited amounts. Once they are mined and used up they cannot be replaced on any human timescale, so they are finite (non-renewable) resources.
bullets: **Ores are finite**: the supply of high-grade ores is running out and remaining ores are often **lower grade** (contain less metal).
Lower-grade ores need **more rock to be mined and processed** per tonne of metal, increasing cost and environmental damage.
Demand for metals keeps rising (electronics, cars, buildings, batteries).
**Recycling** keeps metal in use, so less new ore needs to be extracted and supplies of **valuable raw materials** last longer.
Metals can be recycled **many times** without losing their properties, which makes them ideal for recycling.

callouts.p: Collecting and reprocessing used materials (e.g. melting down scrap metal) so they can be made into new products.
A resource that is used up faster than it can be formed, so it will eventually run out.

core.p: Recycling is a series of steps. Each step has a cost in money, energy and labour, which must be weighed against the savings compared with extracting new metal from ore.
bullets: **Collection**: scrap metal is collected from homes, businesses, scrapyards and recycling centres.
**Transport** to a recycling plant, which uses fuel.
**Sorting**: different metals are separated, e.g. iron and steel using **magnets**, aluminium using other methods (such as eddy current separators) or by hand.
**Shredding and cleaning** to remove paint, plastics and other contaminants.
**Melting** in a furnace and casting into new blocks or sheets for manufacture.
The recycled metal is then made into new products, closing the loop.

callouts.p: Iron and steel are magnetic, so they are easy to separate from aluminium cans using magnets. This is a favourite 1-mark question.

core.p: Most of the environmental benefits come from avoiding mining and extraction, which are the most damaging and energy-hungry stages of a metal's life.
bullets: **Less mining and quarrying**: less destruction of habitats and landscape, less noise, dust and heavy traffic.
**Less waste rock** (spoil heaps) produced - ores often contain only a small percentage of metal.
**Less energy** needed: melting scrap uses much less energy than extracting from ore, so **fewer fossil fuels** are burned.
**Less carbon dioxide** released, so less contribution to **climate change**; also fewer pollutants such as **sulfur dioxide** from processing sulfide ores (acid rain).
**Less landfill**: used metal is not dumped, saving land and avoiding toxic metals leaching into soil and water.
Conserves **finite ores** for the future (sustainable development).

callouts.p: Extracting aluminium by electrolysis uses huge amounts of electricity. Recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of that energy, which is why aluminium cans are so widely recycled.

core.p: Recycling also has money implications. It is not automatically cheaper: a recycling scheme is economically worthwhile only if the savings are greater than the costs of collecting, sorting and processing.
bullets: **Saves money** on mining, transporting ore and the energy for extraction.
**Saves energy costs**, which are a large part of the price of metals like aluminium.
Metals with a **high value** (gold, silver, copper, aluminium) are especially worth recycling.
Creates **jobs** in collection, sorting and reprocessing.
Reduces the need to **import** ores or metals, improving security of supply for a country.
**Costs**: collection schemes, transport, labour for sorting, recycling plants and machinery.
If an ore is **cheap and plentiful** (e.g. iron ore) and the scrap is mixed or contaminated, extraction may sometimes cost less than recycling.

core.p: A good evaluation always includes the downsides. Recycling is not free of environmental impact or cost.
bullets: **Collection and transport** use fuel, releasing CO2 and costing money.
**Sorting** is labour-intensive and needs machinery; mixed metals and alloys are hard to separate.
**Melting still uses energy** (though usually much less than extraction).
Some products are **hard to dismantle**, e.g. electronics with tiny amounts of many metals.
Relies on the **public and businesses** separating and returning their waste.
Recycled metal may contain **impurities**, reducing quality unless further purified.
Recycling plants themselves can produce some **pollution** and noise.

callouts.t: Do not write 'recycling uses no energy'
callouts.p: Recycling uses less energy than extraction, not zero energy. Melting, transport and sorting all need energy.

core.p: The key comparison in exam questions is between making metal from recycled scrap and making it from newly mined ore.
bullets: Extraction: mine ore → transport → concentrate → reduce (carbon or electrolysis) → purify.
Recycling: collect → transport → sort → melt → cast.
Recycling **skips the most energy-intensive step** (reduction of the ore) and removes the mining stage entirely.
The **more reactive** the metal, the **more energy** extraction needs, so the bigger the benefit of recycling (aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, so recycling saves a lot).

core.h: Aluminium: the best case for recycling
core.p: Aluminium is the classic exam example because its extraction is so energy-hungry and the metal is easy to collect in cans and foil.
bullets: Aluminium is extracted by **electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide**, which needs a very large amount of **electricity**.
The aluminium oxide must be melted (dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the operating temperature), adding to energy costs.
Carbon anodes are burned away and must be replaced, releasing CO2.
Recycling aluminium uses only about **5% of the energy** of extraction.
Aluminium does not rust (protective oxide layer), so scrap stays in good condition and is easy to remelt.

callouts.p: 'Explain why recycling aluminium is particularly important' - answer with: extraction by electrolysis uses lots of electricity/energy; recycling uses much less energy; bauxite ore is finite; less mining.

core.p: Steel is the most recycled material in the world by mass, but the economics are different from aluminium.
bullets: Iron is extracted by **reduction with carbon** in a blast furnace, which needs less energy per tonne than electrolysis.
Iron ore is relatively **abundant**, so the price advantage of recycling is smaller than for aluminium.
Scrap steel is **easily separated by magnets**, making sorting cheap.
Recycling steel still saves energy, iron ore, coke (carbon) and limestone, and reduces CO2 emissions.
Scrap steel is often added to new steel during steelmaking.

core.p: Some metals are present in tiny amounts in products, but they are so valuable or scarce that recycling them is very worthwhile.
bullets: **Gold, silver, platinum and copper** in old phones and computers (e-waste) are valuable even in small amounts.
Copper ores are becoming **low grade**, so recycling copper wiring and pipes is economically attractive.
Recovering metals from e-waste also prevents **toxic metals** such as lead and mercury leaching from landfill.
Low-grade ores and waste can also be treated by biological methods (bioleaching, phytoextraction) - covered separately.

core.h: How to evaluate recycling in an exam
core.p: 'Evaluate' means give both advantages and disadvantages and then come to a justified conclusion. Use any data given in the question.
bullets: State **advantages**: conserves finite ores, less energy, less CO2, less mining damage, less landfill, often cheaper, jobs.
State **disadvantages**: collection, transport and sorting costs and energy; melting energy; contamination.
**Use the data**: compare energy, cost or CO2 figures and quote numbers or calculate differences/percentages.
Give a **conclusion**: e.g. 'recycling aluminium is worthwhile because the energy saved is much greater than the energy used in collection'.
Always say **why** something matters (e.g. 'less energy, so fewer fossil fuels burned, so less CO2 released').

callouts.p: Grade 9 answers link the steps: 'less ore mined → less energy for extraction → fewer fossil fuels burned → less CO2 → less global warming'. One link per mark.
