core.p: Recycling is part of using resources sustainably - meeting the needs of people today without stopping future generations meeting their own needs.
bullets: Reduce, **reuse**, recycle: reusing an item (e.g. refilling a container) usually saves even more energy than recycling it.
Recycling metals reduces our dependence on **finite** ores.
Life-cycle assessments (covered separately) can be used to compare a recycled product with one made from new materials.

callouts.p: Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

analogy.t: Refilling a water bottle instead of digging a new well
analogy.p: Mining and extracting a metal is like digging a new well every time you want a drink: hard work, lots of energy, and it damages the land, and eventually the water table runs dry (finite ores). Recycling is like refilling the bottle you already have: you still have to walk to the tap (collection and transport) and run the tap (melting), but it costs far less effort. Where it breaks down: refilling is always easier, but recycling is not always cheaper - if the scrap is scattered, mixed or contaminated, or the ore is very cheap, the walk to the tap can cost more than the new well.

terms.d: Collecting and reprocessing used materials, such as melting scrap metal, so they can be made into new products.
A resource that will run out because it is used faster than it is formed, e.g. metal ores.
A rock containing enough metal or metal compound to make extracting the metal economically worthwhile.
An ore that contains only a small percentage of metal, so more rock must be processed per tonne of metal.
The natural substances (e.g. ores, fossil fuels) used to make a product.
Used or waste metal that can be recycled.
Obtaining a metal from its ore, by reduction with carbon or by electrolysis.
Using electricity to decompose an ionic compound; used to extract reactive metals like aluminium and needs a lot of energy.
Disposal of waste by burying it in the ground; uses land and can release pollutants.
Meeting the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
The effects on costs, prices, profits and jobs.
The effects on habitats, pollution, energy use, emissions and waste.
A pile of waste rock left over from mining an ore.
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment, containing valuable and toxic metals.

mistakes.w: Recycling uses no energy.
mistakes.r: Recycling uses less energy than extracting metal from ore, but collection, transport, sorting and melting still need energy.

mistakes.w: Recycling is always cheaper.
mistakes.r: Recycling is often cheaper, but collection, sorting and transport costs can make it less economic for cheap, abundant metals or mixed scrap.

mistakes.w: Recycling stops pollution.
mistakes.r: Recycling reduces pollution (e.g. less CO2 and SO2 from extraction), but transport and melting still produce some.

mistakes.w: Recycling is good because it is better for the environment.
mistakes.r: Give a specific reason, e.g. less ore needs to be mined, so less habitat destruction and less waste rock.

mistakes.w: Metals are renewable because they can be recycled.
mistakes.r: Metal ores are finite (non-renewable); recycling makes the supply last longer but does not create new ore.

mistakes.w: Recycling saves energy because metal is already made.
mistakes.r: Recycling saves energy because the energy-intensive extraction step (reducing the ore by carbon or electrolysis) is not needed.

mistakes.w: Less landfill means less global warming.
mistakes.r: Less landfill saves land and reduces leaching of toxic metals; the reduction in CO2 comes mainly from using less energy (fewer fossil fuels burned).

mistakes.w: Aluminium is recycled because it rusts.
mistakes.r: Aluminium does not rust; it is recycled mainly because its extraction by electrolysis uses so much electricity.

exam.q: Give one reason why metals should be recycled.
model: Any one: metal ores are finite / conserves ores; saves energy; less mining; less landfill; less CO2 released.
exam.tip: One clear, specific reason is enough for 1 mark.

exam.q: Describe how iron and steel can be separated from aluminium in a recycling plant.
model: Using a magnet (iron and steel are magnetic, aluminium is not).
exam.tip: Name the method and, if you can, the property it relies on.

exam.q: Explain why recycling aluminium saves more energy than extracting it from its ore.
model: Extraction of aluminium uses electrolysis, which needs a lot of (electrical) energy.
Recycling only needs energy to melt the aluminium (and transport), which is much less.
exam.tip: Compare the two processes; do not just state that recycling saves energy.

exam.q: Explain two environmental advantages of recycling copper rather than extracting it from copper ore.
model: Less copper ore needs to be mined (1).
So less damage to habitats / landscape / less waste rock (1).
Less energy is needed (1).
So fewer fossil fuels burned / less carbon dioxide released / less global warming (1).
exam.tip: 'Explain two' with 4 marks = point + consequence for each.

exam.q: Suggest two reasons why recycling metals can sometimes be expensive.
model: Cost of collecting and transporting scrap.
Cost of sorting / separating different metals (labour, machinery) or removing impurities.
exam.tip: Think about every step from bin to furnace.

exam.q: State why metal ores are described as finite resources.
model: They will run out / are not being replaced (as fast as they are used).
exam.tip: Finite means limited supply that will eventually be used up.

exam.q: Gold is present in very small amounts in mobile phones. Suggest why it is still worthwhile to recycle the gold.
model: Gold is very valuable / expensive.
Gold ores are scarce/finite, so recycling conserves supplies (and avoids mining large amounts of rock).
exam.tip: Link the value of the metal to the economics of recycling.

exam.q: Extracting 1 tonne of a metal from its ore uses 200 GJ of energy. Recycling 1 tonne uses 10 GJ. Calculate the percentage of energy saved by recycling.
model: Energy saved = 200 - 10 = 190 GJ.
Percentage saved = 190 / 200 x 100 = 95%.
exam.tip: Percentage saved = (saving / original) x 100. Use the original (extraction) value as the denominator.

exam.q: Explain why recycling iron is less economically important than recycling aluminium.
model: Iron is extracted by reduction with carbon, which uses less energy than electrolysis.
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, which uses a large amount of electricity (so is expensive).
So the cost/energy saving from recycling aluminium is much greater (iron ore is also more abundant/cheaper).
exam.tip: Link the extraction method to energy and cost.

exam.q: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of recycling metals. Refer to economic and environmental factors in your answer.
model: Advantage: conserves finite metal ores for the future.
Advantage: less mining, so less habitat destruction, noise and waste rock.
Advantage: less energy than extraction, so fewer fossil fuels burned and less CO2 (and SO2) released.
Advantage: less waste in landfill; often cheaper than extraction; creates jobs.
Disadvantage: collection, transport and sorting cost money and use energy/fuel; melting still uses energy; mixed or contaminated scrap is hard to process.
Conclusion: overall recycling is usually worthwhile, especially for metals extracted by electrolysis (aluminium) or valuable metals (gold, copper), because savings outweigh costs.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs both sides, economic AND environmental points, and a justified conclusion.

worked.q: A council collects 500 tonnes of aluminium cans. Making 1 tonne of aluminium from ore releases 12 tonnes of CO2; recycling 1 tonne releases 0.6 tonnes. Calculate the mass of CO2 saved by recycling the cans instead of using new aluminium.
steps: CO2 if made from ore = 500 x 12 = 6000 tonnes.
CO2 if recycled = 500 x 0.6 = 300 tonnes.
CO2 saved = 6000 - 300 = 5700 tonnes.
Percentage saved = 5700 / 6000 x 100 = 95%.
worked.ans: 5700 tonnes of CO2 saved (a 95% reduction).

worked.q: A company can buy new copper from ore for £6000 per tonne. Recycled copper costs £1200 per tonne to collect and transport, £800 per tonne to sort and £1500 per tonne to melt and purify. Is recycling economically worthwhile? Give two environmental reasons that support your conclusion.
steps: Total cost of recycling = 1200 + 800 + 1500 = £3500 per tonne.
Saving = 6000 - 3500 = £2500 per tonne, so recycling is cheaper.
Environmental reason 1: less copper ore mined, so less habitat damage and waste rock.
Environmental reason 2: less energy used, so less fossil fuel burned and less CO2 released.
Conclusion: recycling is both economically and environmentally worthwhile here.
worked.ans: Yes: recycling costs £3500 per tonne, saving £2500 per tonne, and it reduces mining damage and CO2 emissions.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why recycling metals helps to preserve the supply of valuable raw materials.
steps: Metals are obtained from ores, which are finite resources in the Earth's crust.
High-grade ores are running out, and lower-grade ores need more mining and energy.
Recycling returns metal from used products to manufacturing.
So less new ore needs to be extracted, and existing reserves last longer for future generations.
worked.ans: Recycling reduces the amount of finite ore that needs to be mined, so reserves of valuable ores last longer.

chem_edx.4.5.summary: A **life-cycle assessment (LCA)** looks at the environmental impact of a product over its whole life, from **obtaining the raw materials**, through **manufacturing** and **using** the product, to **disposing** of it at the end of its useful life. At each stage it considers the **energy, water and other resources** used and the **pollution and waste** produced. You must be able to **evaluate LCA data** to compare products, and to recognise that LCAs have limits: some effects are hard to measure, so they involve **value judgements**, and LCAs can be **selective or biased**.

core.p: A life-cycle assessment is a 'cradle to grave' analysis of a product. Instead of judging a product only by how it is made or how it is thrown away, an LCA adds up its environmental effects at every stage so that different products can be compared fairly.
bullets: Assesses the **environmental impact** of a product over its **whole life**.
Used by manufacturers, governments and consumers to **compare** products or materials (e.g. paper vs plastic bags).
Helps identify **which stage** causes most harm, so that stage can be improved.
Considers effects such as **energy use, use of resources, pollution of air, water and land, and waste**.
Transport between stages is included and can be significant.

callouts.p: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product at each stage of its life: obtaining the raw materials, manufacturing the product, using the product and disposing of the product when it is no longer useful.

core.p: Every product starts with raw materials taken from the Earth. Extracting and processing them often has a big environmental impact.
bullets: Examples: **mining** metal ores, **drilling** for crude oil, **felling** trees for paper, quarrying limestone.
Uses up **finite resources** such as ores and crude oil.
**Damages habitats** and landscapes; produces waste rock and noise.
Needs **energy** for extraction and processing (e.g. extracting a metal, fractional distillation and cracking of crude oil).
Can cause **pollution**, e.g. CO2 from burning fuels, SO2 from processing sulfide ores.

core.p: Turning the raw materials into a finished, packaged product uses energy and other resources and produces waste.
bullets: Uses **energy** (often from fossil fuels) for factory processes.
Uses **water** and other chemicals.
Produces **waste products** and by-products, some toxic; pollution of air and water.
Packaging adds extra materials and waste.
Some waste can be reduced or turned into useful products (e.g. off-cuts recycled within the factory).

core.p: The use stage depends on what the product is. For some products it is tiny; for others it is the biggest part of the whole life cycle.
bullets: Products that **use energy** while in use (cars, washing machines, kettles) can have their largest impact at this stage, e.g. a car burns fuel throughout its life.
Products that need **maintenance**, cleaning or replacement parts add impact (e.g. washing reusable nappies).
Some products have very little impact in use (e.g. a chair or a shopping bag).
**How long** the product lasts and **how many times** it is used matter: a longer-lasting product spreads its manufacturing impact over more uses.

callouts.p: When comparing reusable and disposable products, compare the impact per use. A cotton bag has a higher impact to make, but it can be used many times.

core.h: Stage 4: disposal at end of life
core.p: When the product is no longer useful it must be disposed of. The method of disposal changes the overall impact.
bullets: **Landfill**: uses land; some materials (e.g. many plastics) do not biodegrade; toxic substances may leach into soil and water; biodegradable waste can release methane.
**Incineration (burning)**: reduces landfill and can generate electricity, but releases CO2 and possibly toxic gases.
**Recycling or reuse**: reduces the need for new raw materials and energy, but collection and processing still have impacts.
Transport to the disposal site uses fuel.
Products that are **easy to recycle or biodegradable** usually score better at this stage.

core.p: At each of the four stages the LCA records the inputs taken from the environment and the outputs released into it.
bullets: **Inputs**: energy (often in MJ), water (litres), raw materials (kg).
**Outputs**: greenhouse gases such as CO2 (kg), other air pollutants (e.g. SO2, NOx), water pollutants, solid waste (kg).
Data are usually given **per item** or per unit of use, so products can be compared.
The **total** for each type of effect is found by adding the values for every stage.

core.p: Some environmental effects can be measured accurately and given a number. Others cannot easily be measured, so whoever writes the LCA has to decide how important they are - this is a value judgement.
bullets: **Easy to quantify**: energy used, mass of CO2 emitted, volume of water used, mass of waste produced.
**Hard to quantify**: visual pollution, noise, smell, effect on wildlife and habitats, effects on human health, effects that happen far in the future.
Allocating numbers to these needs **value judgements**, which are **subjective** - different people may give different values.
So an LCA is **not a purely objective process**, and two LCAs of the same product can reach different conclusions.

callouts.p: A decision based on opinion about how important something is, rather than on measured data.

core.p: Because LCAs involve choices and judgements, their conclusions must be checked carefully. Edexcel questions often ask you to evaluate whether an LCA is reliable.
bullets: **Selective LCAs**: a company may include only the stages or effects that make its product look good (e.g. for advertising).
**Who paid for it?** An LCA funded by the manufacturer may be **biased**.
**Assumptions**: e.g. how many times a bag is reused, how far it is transported, whether it is recycled.
**Incomplete data**: some impacts are unknown or estimated.
**Different units** or effects can be hard to compare (is 1 kg less CO2 better than 10 litres less water?).
A full, **independent** LCA covering **all stages and all effects** is more reliable.

callouts.p: Do not claim an LCA 'proves' a product is better. Say the data suggest it has a lower impact for the effects measured, and mention any limitations.

core.p: Spec point 4.12 asks you to evaluate data from an LCA. Follow a clear method so that you use the numbers and make a justified judgement.
bullets: **Read the table carefully**: check units and whether values are per item or per use.
**Compare stage by stage**: which product has the larger impact at each stage, and why?
**Calculate totals or differences** where possible (e.g. total CO2 for each product).
**Look for trade-offs**: one product may use more energy but produce less solid waste.
Consider **missing information** and **value judgements**: what has not been included?
**Conclude**: state which product has the lower overall environmental impact, quoting data, and explain any reservations.

callouts.p: Marks for evaluation questions usually need data from the table, e.g. 'the plastic bag produces 1.6 kg CO2 compared with 3.3 kg for the paper bag'.

core.h: Classic example: plastic vs paper shopping bags
core.p: A common exam comparison. The numbers below are illustrative of the kind of data given; always use the data in the question.
bullets: Plastic (poly(ethene)) bags are made from **crude oil**, a finite resource; paper bags from **wood**, a renewable resource.
Paper bags are heavier, so need **more energy and water** to make and transport.
Plastic bags are **not biodegradable** and persist in landfill and the environment; paper bags **biodegrade** and are more easily recycled.
Plastic bags are stronger and can be **reused** many times, reducing impact per use.
So neither is simply 'better': the answer depends on **which effects** you weigh most heavily - a value judgement.

head: Stage / effect
Plastic bag
Paper bag
rows: Crude oil (finite); fractional distillation and cracking
Non-biodegradable; can be recycled but often not

core.p: Recycling changes the disposal stage and also reduces the raw materials stage for the next product, which is why LCAs often favour recyclable materials.
bullets: Recycling reduces the need to **extract new raw materials**, saving energy and finite resources.
It reduces **landfill** at the disposal stage.
But collection, transport and reprocessing add impacts that must be included.
An LCA can show whether recycling a product really saves more than it costs.

core.p: Six-mark 'evaluate' or 'compare' questions are level-marked. The top level needs data used throughout and a supported conclusion.
bullets: Work through the **four stages** in order, comparing the products at each.
Use **comparative words**: more, less, higher, lower, and quote values.
Include at least one **calculation** if possible (totals or differences).
Mention **renewable vs finite** raw materials and **biodegradable vs non-biodegradable** disposal where relevant.
Finish with a **conclusion** and one **limitation** (e.g. value judgements, missing data, assumptions about reuse).

callouts.p: Raw materials, manufacture, use, disposal. Learn them in order - many 1 and 2 mark questions simply ask you to name them.

analogy.p: An LCA is like writing a full biography of a product rather than just a snapshot. A photo of a shiny new car in the showroom tells you nothing about the mine its steel came from, the fuel it burns for 15 years, or the scrapyard at the end. The biography follows it from birth (raw materials) to death (disposal) and adds up its 'footprint' at each chapter. Where it breaks down: a biography is a story told by an author, and with an LCA too the author chooses what to include and how important each effect is - which is exactly why LCAs can be biased, whereas the analogy makes it sound like a complete, neutral record.

terms.d: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product over its whole life: raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal.
Describes an analysis that covers a product from extraction of raw materials to final disposal.
The natural substances (e.g. ores, crude oil, timber) extracted to make a product.
The stage in which raw materials are processed into the finished, packaged product.
What happens to a product at the end of its useful life: landfill, incineration, reuse or recycling.
A resource that will run out because it is used faster than it is replaced, e.g. crude oil.
A resource that can be replaced as fast as it is used, e.g. timber from managed forests.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms in the environment.
Disposal of waste by burying it in the ground.
Disposal of waste by burning it, which can generate energy but releases gases such as CO2.
A decision based on opinion about how important an effect is, rather than on measurement.
Able to be measured and expressed as a number, e.g. energy in MJ or mass of CO2 in kg.
An LCA that includes only some stages or effects, often to make a product look better; may be biased.
A one-sided view, e.g. an LCA written to support a company's product.
The effect of human activity on the environment, e.g. pollution, resource use, habitat loss.

mistakes.w: The stages are making, selling and throwing away.
mistakes.r: The four stages are obtaining raw materials, manufacturing the product, using the product and disposing of it.

mistakes.w: An LCA looks at the cost of a product.
mistakes.r: An LCA assesses environmental impact (energy, resources, pollution, waste), not price or profit.

mistakes.w: An LCA is completely objective.
mistakes.r: Some effects (e.g. visual pollution) cannot be measured, so values are assigned by value judgement; LCAs can be subjective or biased.

mistakes.w: Paper bags are better because paper is natural.
mistakes.r: Paper comes from a renewable resource and biodegrades, but needs more energy and water to make; use the data to compare overall impact.

mistakes.w: The product with the lowest manufacturing energy is best.
mistakes.r: Compare the totals across all stages; a product may be low at one stage but high at another (e.g. during use).

mistakes.w: Recycling has no environmental impact.
mistakes.r: Recycling reduces impact but collection, transport and reprocessing still use energy and cause some pollution.

mistakes.w: Companies always produce accurate LCAs.
mistakes.r: LCAs produced by manufacturers may be selective or biased to support their product's claims.

mistakes.w: Plastic is bad because it is made from chemicals.
mistakes.r: Plastic is made from crude oil, a finite resource, and most plastics are not biodegradable, so they persist in landfill and the environment.

exam.q: State the four stages considered in a life-cycle assessment.
model: Obtaining raw materials and manufacturing the product (1).
Using the product and disposing of it (1).
exam.tip: Typically 1 mark for each pair of stages; learn them in order.

exam.q: Give one environmental impact of obtaining the raw materials to make a steel product.
model: Any one: habitat destruction from mining; waste rock / spoil heaps; uses finite iron ore; energy use / CO2 emissions from extraction.
exam.tip: Be specific to the stage asked about.

exam.q: Suggest why the use stage of a car has a large environmental impact, but the use stage of a wooden table does not.
model: A car burns fuel throughout its life, releasing CO2 / pollutants / using finite resources.
A table needs no energy (or little maintenance) while being used.
exam.tip: Compare both products in your answer.

exam.q: Explain why some LCAs are described as biased.
model: They may be produced by (or paid for by) the manufacturer / be selective, including only some effects or stages.
So they may make the product seem to have less environmental impact than it really has.
exam.tip: Give the cause of bias and its effect on the conclusion.

exam.q: Explain why it is difficult to give numerical values to some effects in a life-cycle assessment.
model: Some effects, e.g. visual pollution / noise / effect on wildlife, cannot be measured easily.
So values must be decided by value judgement, which is subjective (different people give different values).
exam.tip: Name an example of a hard-to-measure effect.

exam.q: An LCA for a drinks bottle gives: raw materials 4.2 MJ, manufacture 6.8 MJ, use 0.0 MJ, disposal 1.5 MJ. Calculate the total energy used.
exam.tip: Include units in your final answer.

exam.q: Using the table of plastic and paper bag data in the question, give two advantages of paper bags over plastic bags.
model: Made from a renewable resource (wood) rather than finite crude oil.
Biodegradable / more easily recycled, so less long-lasting waste in landfill.
exam.tip: Advantages must be comparative: 'paper is biodegradable but plastic is not'.

exam.q: Product X releases 8 kg of CO2 during manufacture and 2 kg during disposal. Product Y releases 5 kg during manufacture and 6 kg during disposal. Both release no CO2 in use. Which product releases less CO2 overall? Show your working.
model: X total = 8 + 2 = 10 kg; Y total = 5 + 6 = 11 kg.
Product X releases less CO2 overall (by 1 kg).
exam.tip: Always calculate totals before choosing; the lowest single stage does not decide it.

exam.q: Suggest one reason why a life-cycle assessment for a reusable cotton bag might differ depending on who carried it out.
model: Different assumptions about how many times it is reused / value judgements about the importance of effects / selective choice of data.
exam.tip: Think about the assumptions that the result depends on.

exam.q: A company claims its new plastic packaging is better for the environment than glass. Evaluate how a life-cycle assessment could be used to test this claim, and the limitations of doing so.
model: An LCA would compare both packaging types at every stage: raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal.
Raw materials: plastic from finite crude oil; glass from sand and limestone (abundant but quarried).
Manufacture: compare energy used and pollution; glass needs very high temperatures; plastic is lighter so transport uses less fuel.
Disposal: glass is easily recycled; most plastic is not biodegradable but can be recycled.
Limitations: some effects need value judgements; data may be incomplete; LCA by the company may be selective or biased.
Conclusion: an independent, full LCA using quantified data is needed before accepting the claim.
exam.tip: Cover all four stages for both products, include limitations, and end with a justified conclusion.

worked.q: Use the LCA data to decide which of two kettles has the lower environmental impact. Kettle P: raw materials 20 MJ, manufacture 35 MJ, use 900 MJ, disposal 5 MJ. Kettle Q: raw materials 30 MJ, manufacture 50 MJ, use 760 MJ, disposal 4 MJ.
steps: Q uses more energy to make (80 MJ vs 55 MJ) but much less in use (760 MJ vs 900 MJ).
The use stage dominates for both kettles, so the more efficient kettle in use wins overall.
Difference = 960 - 844 = 116 MJ in favour of Q.
worked.ans: Kettle Q has the lower total energy use (844 MJ vs 960 MJ), because it uses less energy during the use stage, which is the largest stage.

worked.q: A disposable plastic bag releases 1.6 kg CO2 over its life and is used once. A cotton bag releases 60 kg CO2 over its life. How many times must the cotton bag be used to have a lower CO2 impact per use than the disposable bag?
steps: Per use, the plastic bag = 1.6 kg CO2 (used once).
Cotton bag per use = 60 / n, where n = number of uses.
So the cotton bag must be used at least 38 times.
worked.ans: At least 38 uses; this shows the result depends on the assumption about reuse, a key limitation of LCAs.

worked.q: Model answer: describe what a life-cycle assessment of a mobile phone would consider.
steps: Raw materials: mining metals such as copper, gold and lithium (finite, habitat damage, energy) and crude oil for plastic casing.
Manufacture: energy and water used in making components and assembling; chemical waste; packaging.
Use: electricity to charge the phone over its life.
Disposal: landfill (toxic metals may leach), or recycling to recover valuable metals.
At each stage: energy, resources used, pollution and waste, plus transport between stages.
worked.ans: An LCA would assess the environmental impact of raw materials, manufacture, use (charging) and disposal or recycling of the phone, including energy, resources, pollution and waste at each stage.

chem_edx.4.6.summary: Many chemical reactions are **reversible**: the products can react to re-form the original reactants, and we show this with the symbol ⇌. The direction of some reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions, for example heating ammonium chloride or hydrated copper sulfate. In a **closed system** a reversible reaction reaches **dynamic equilibrium**, where the forward and reverse reactions are still happening but at the **same rate**, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay **constant**.

core.p: Most reactions you meet seem to go one way only, but in a **reversible reaction** the products can react together to make the original reactants again. The reaction from left to right is the **forward reaction**; the reaction from right to left is the **reverse (backward) reaction**.
bullets: General form: A + B ⇌ C + D
Forward reaction: A + B → C + D (reactants make products)
Reverse reaction: C + D → A + B (products make reactants again)
Both reactions involve the **same substances**, just in opposite directions
The symbol ⇌ (two half arrows) means the reaction is **reversible**
A one-way arrow → is used for reactions that are not reversible (in practice), such as burning methane

callouts.p: A reaction in which the products can react to form the original reactants again.
⇌ shows a reaction is reversible. Always draw it with two half arrows, one pointing each way.

core.h: The ⇌ symbol and how to read equations
core.p: When you see ⇌ in an equation you must think of two reactions happening, not one. Exam questions often ask you to identify the reversible reaction from a list of equations, or to explain what the symbol means.
bullets: Read 'N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3' as: nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia, AND ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen
The left side is called the **reactants side** (or left-hand side), the right side the **products side**
State symbols are still used: NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)
Word equations can also use the symbol: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride
The equation must still be **balanced**: atoms are conserved in both directions

callouts.p: For 'What does ⇌ mean?' write: the reaction is reversible / the reaction can go in both directions. 'Equilibrium' alone does not score the mark.

core.h: Changing the conditions changes the direction
core.p: The spec says the **direction of some reversible reactions can be altered by changing the reaction conditions**. Heating usually pushes a reaction in the endothermic direction; cooling lets the exothermic direction take over. Adding or removing a substance (such as water) can also change which way the reaction goes.
bullets: Conditions that can change direction: **temperature**, **pressure** (for gases) and **concentration** (adding or removing a substance)
Heating ammonium chloride makes it decompose; cooling the gases makes the solid form again
Heating blue hydrated copper sulfate drives off water and leaves white anhydrous copper sulfate; adding water turns it blue again
This is why we say these reactions are 'reversible by changing conditions'
How far the position of equilibrium moves is covered in spec point 4.17

core.p: Ammonium chloride is a white solid. When it is heated at the bottom of a test tube it **thermally decomposes** into two colourless gases, ammonia and hydrogen chloride. These gases rise to the cooler top of the tube, where they **react together again** to re-form white solid ammonium chloride.
bullets: Equation: NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)
Forward reaction (hot end): ammonium chloride → ammonia + hydrogen chloride, which is **endothermic** (takes in heat)
Reverse reaction (cool end): ammonia + hydrogen chloride → ammonium chloride, which is **exothermic** (gives out heat)
Observation: the white solid at the bottom disappears and a **white solid forms near the top** of the tube
The tube is open so this is not a closed system: equilibrium is not reached here
Safety: ammonia and hydrogen chloride are both harmful/irritant gases, so use a fume cupboard or a loose plug of mineral wool

callouts.p: The white solid at the top is not ammonium chloride that has just sublimed. It is new ammonium chloride made by a chemical reaction between two gases.

core.h: Example 2: hydrated and anhydrous copper sulfate
core.p: Blue copper sulfate crystals contain **water of crystallisation**; this form is called **hydrated** copper sulfate. Heating it drives off the water and leaves a white powder called **anhydrous** copper sulfate. Adding water back turns the white powder blue again and the mixture gets hot.
bullets: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)
Word equation: hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water
Forward reaction (heating) is **endothermic**: energy must be supplied
Reverse reaction (adding water) is **exothermic**: the same amount of energy is given out
Colour change white to blue is used as a **test for water** (it shows water is present, not that it is pure)
Same idea: hydrated cobalt chloride is pink, anhydrous cobalt chloride is blue

callouts.p: If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction.

core.p: Equilibrium can only be reached in a **closed system**. This means nothing (no reactants or products) can get in or out, although energy can still be transferred to or from the surroundings. In an open test tube, gases escape so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace and equilibrium is never set up.
bullets: Closed system: a sealed container where **no substances can enter or leave**
Example: a stoppered flask, a sealed syringe of gas, or a reaction vessel in industry where products are kept in contact with reactants
Open system example: heating calcium carbonate in an open crucible, where carbon dioxide escapes
If a product escapes, the reverse reaction cannot happen, so the reaction goes to completion instead

callouts.p: A system in which no substances can enter or leave (energy can still be transferred).

core.p: When a reversible reaction happens in a closed system, it eventually reaches a state called **dynamic equilibrium**. Both reactions are still happening, but because they happen at the **same rate**, the amounts of reactants and products do not change. The word **dynamic** means the reactions have not stopped; the word **equilibrium** means there is a balance.
bullets: The **forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate**
The **concentrations of reactants and products remain constant** (they do not change)
Both reactions are **still occurring** (it is dynamic, not static)
It can only be reached in a **closed system**
Concentrations are constant, but they are **not necessarily equal**
At equilibrium nothing appears to be happening on the large scale (no colour change, no pressure change), even though particles keep reacting

callouts.p: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
'The reaction has stopped' scores zero. Equilibrium means both reactions continue at equal rates.

core.h: How equilibrium is reached: rates over time
core.p: At the start only reactants are present, so the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction has a rate of zero. As reactants are used up, the forward rate falls. As products build up, the reverse rate rises. Eventually the two rates become equal: equilibrium has been reached and the rates then stay equal.
bullets: Start: high concentration of reactants, so frequent successful collisions and a **fast forward rate**
Start: no products, so **reverse rate = 0**
Over time: reactant concentration falls, so forward rate **decreases**
Over time: product concentration rises, so reverse rate **increases**
Equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate, both lines on the graph become **flat and meet**
This reasoning uses collision theory: rate depends on how often reacting particles collide

callouts.p: Link each change in rate to a change in concentration (WHY), then finish with the two equilibrium statements: rates equal, concentrations constant.

core.p: On a concentration against time graph, the reactant line falls and the product line rises until both become **horizontal**. Flat lines mean the concentrations are constant. They usually flatten at **different heights**, because the position of equilibrium may lie towards the reactants or towards the products.
bullets: Reactant concentration: starts high, falls, then levels off
Product concentration: starts at zero, rises, then levels off
Both level off **at the same time**, the moment equilibrium is reached
If the products line ends higher, the equilibrium lies to the **right** (more products)
If the reactants line ends higher, the equilibrium lies to the **left** (more reactants)

callouts.p: Do not say the amounts of reactants and products are equal at equilibrium. They are constant (unchanging).

core.p: Imagine watching individual particles in a sealed flask at equilibrium. Some reactant particles are colliding and turning into products; at exactly the same time, some product particles are turning back into reactants. Because these happen equally often, the total number of each type of particle stays the same.
bullets: Individual particles keep changing between reactant and product
The **numbers** of each type of particle stay constant overall
If radioactive (labelled) atoms were added, they would spread into both reactants and products, which is evidence the equilibrium is dynamic
Macroscopic properties (colour, pressure, concentration) are constant at equilibrium

core.p: The same equilibrium can be reached by starting with the reactants or by starting with the products, as long as the conditions (temperature, pressure) and the overall amounts of atoms are the same. This shows that both directions are genuinely possible.
bullets: Start with only N2 and H2: the forward reaction makes NH3 until equilibrium
Start with only NH3: the reverse reaction makes N2 and H2 until the same equilibrium is reached
At equilibrium, the mixture contains **all** the substances in the equation
A reversible reaction in a closed system never gives a 100% yield of product

head: Feature
Reaction going to completion
Reversible reaction at equilibrium
rows: Yes, forward and reverse at equal rates
Must be closed to reach equilibrium

core.p: Many important industrial reactions are reversible, the most famous being the **Haber process** to make ammonia (spec points 4.15 to 4.16). Because the reaction reaches equilibrium, not all the reactants turn into product, so chemists choose conditions that give an acceptable amount of product at an acceptable rate.
bullets: Haber process: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)
Industry removes the product and recycles unreacted reactants, so the system is not left at equilibrium
Changing the conditions changes where the equilibrium lies (spec point 4.17)
A catalyst makes equilibrium be reached faster but does not change the amounts at equilibrium

callouts.p: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the position of equilibrium is unchanged.

analogy.p: Imagine running up a down escalator at exactly the same speed as it moves down. You are working hard and the steps are constantly moving, yet you stay in the same place. That is dynamic equilibrium: two opposite processes happening at the same rate, so nothing seems to change overall. A better match for concentrations: two shops in a shopping centre where people walk from shop A to shop B at the same rate as others walk from B to A; the number in each shop stays constant even though people keep moving, and the two shops need not hold the same number of people. Where it breaks down: people choose to move, whereas particles react only when they collide with enough energy, and the rates in a reaction depend on concentration, which changes until equilibrium is reached.

terms.d: A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants.
The symbol showing that a reaction is reversible (can go in both directions).
The reaction from left to right in the equation: reactants forming products.
The reaction from right to left in the equation: products forming the original reactants.
A system where no substances can enter or leave; needed for equilibrium to be reached.
The state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
Still moving or happening: at equilibrium both reactions continue.
The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium (lying to the left or to the right).
Containing water of crystallisation, e.g. blue hydrated copper sulfate CuSO4.5H2O.
Without water of crystallisation, e.g. white anhydrous copper sulfate CuSO4.
Water molecules that are part of the structure of a crystal.
Breaking down a substance into simpler substances using heat, e.g. ammonium chloride into ammonia and hydrogen chloride.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
A reaction that gives out energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up; it does not change the position of equilibrium.

mistakes.w: At equilibrium the reaction has stopped.
mistakes.r: Both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate.

mistakes.w: At equilibrium there are equal amounts of reactants and products.
mistakes.r: The concentrations of reactants and products are constant, not necessarily equal.

mistakes.w: The rates are constant at equilibrium.
mistakes.r: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal (to each other).

mistakes.w: Equilibrium can be reached in any container.
mistakes.r: Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system, where no substances can escape.

mistakes.w: The white solid at the top of the tube is ammonium chloride that has evaporated.
mistakes.r: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases react together in the cooler part of the tube to re-form solid ammonium chloride.

mistakes.w: Both directions of a reversible reaction are exothermic.
mistakes.r: If one direction is exothermic the other is endothermic, and the same amount of energy is transferred.

mistakes.w: Adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate turns it white.
mistakes.r: Anhydrous copper sulfate is white and turns blue when water is added; heating blue hydrated copper sulfate turns it white.

mistakes.w: A catalyst gives more product at equilibrium.
mistakes.r: A catalyst only makes equilibrium be reached faster; it does not change the position of equilibrium.

exam.q: What does the symbol ⇌ mean in a chemical equation?
model: The reaction is reversible / can go in both directions.
exam.tip: Do not just write 'equilibrium'.

exam.q: Ammonium chloride is heated in a test tube. A white solid forms near the top of the tube. Explain this observation.
model: Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating to form ammonia and hydrogen chloride (gases).
The gases rise to the cooler part of the tube.
They react / recombine to re-form (white solid) ammonium chloride; the reaction is reversible.
exam.tip: Mention both gases by name and that it is the reverse reaction at the cool end.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reversible decomposition of ammonium chloride.
model: NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl with correct reversible arrow.
Correct state symbols: (s) ⇌ (g) + (g).
exam.tip: The reversible arrow is required for the first mark.

exam.q: Describe what you would see when water is added to white anhydrous copper sulfate, and state what happens to the temperature.
model: Turns (from white) to blue.
Temperature increases / gets hot / exothermic.
exam.tip: Give the colour change from and to.

exam.q: The reaction hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water is endothermic in the forward direction. State what this tells you about the reverse reaction.
model: The reverse reaction is exothermic.
The same amount of energy is transferred (given out) as is taken in by the forward reaction.
exam.tip: Two marks: name it AND state 'same amount'.

exam.q: State two features of a system at dynamic equilibrium.
model: Rate of forward reaction equals rate of reverse reaction.
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant / do not change.
exam.tip: 'Equal concentrations' loses the mark.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by 'dynamic' in the term dynamic equilibrium.
model: The forward and reverse reactions are still happening / have not stopped.
exam.tip: Keep it to the idea of continuing reactions.

exam.q: Why can dynamic equilibrium only be reached in a closed system?
model: In an open system products (or reactants) can escape.
So the reverse reaction cannot occur at the same rate / the reaction would not reach equilibrium.
exam.tip: Link escaping substances to the reverse reaction.

exam.q: Nitrogen and hydrogen are sealed in a container and react to form ammonia. Describe and explain how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions change from the start until equilibrium is reached.
model: At the start the forward rate is high because the concentration of nitrogen and hydrogen is high.
Forward rate decreases as nitrogen and hydrogen are used up / their concentration falls.
Reverse rate starts at zero and increases as the concentration of ammonia increases.
At equilibrium the rates of forward and reverse reactions become equal (and then stay the same).
exam.tip: Each change of rate needs a reason linked to concentration.

exam.q: Explain why a reversible reaction in a closed system can never give a 100% yield of product.
model: As product forms, some of it reacts in the reverse reaction to re-form the reactants.
Equilibrium is reached with reactants and products both present, so not all reactants are converted.
exam.tip: Mention that reactants remain at equilibrium.

exam.q: A student says: 'At equilibrium nothing is happening because the colour of the mixture stays the same.' Evaluate this statement.
model: The student is correct that the colour / concentrations stay constant.
But reactions are still happening: it is a dynamic equilibrium.
The forward and reverse reactions are happening at the same rate.
So substances are made and used up at the same rate, giving no overall change.
exam.tip: Evaluate means say what is right AND what is wrong, then conclude.

worked.q: Explain fully the observations when blue hydrated copper sulfate is heated in a test tube and then, after cooling, water is added to the residue.
steps: Heating supplies energy, so the endothermic forward reaction takes place: CuSO4.5H2O → CuSO4 + 5H2O.
Water of crystallisation is driven off as steam (condensation may be seen near the top of the tube) and the solid turns from blue to white.
The white solid is anhydrous copper sulfate.
When water is added, the reverse reaction happens: CuSO4 + 5H2O → CuSO4.5H2O.
The solid turns blue again and the tube becomes hot because the reverse reaction is exothermic.
The energy given out equals the energy taken in by the forward reaction.
worked.ans: Blue to white on heating (endothermic, water lost); white to blue on adding water with the tube getting hot (exothermic, same energy released). This shows the reaction is reversible and its direction is changed by changing the conditions.

worked.q: A reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) is set up in a sealed flask starting with 1.00 mol of A. After 10 minutes the flask contains 0.40 mol of A and 0.60 mol of B. After 20 minutes it still contains 0.40 mol of A and 0.60 mol of B. Explain what this shows and why the student who says 'the reaction stopped at 10 minutes' is wrong.
steps: The amounts did not change between 10 and 20 minutes, so the concentrations are constant.
In a closed system this shows equilibrium had been reached by 10 minutes.
Total moles: 0.40 + 0.60 = 1.00 mol, so the atoms are conserved and the flask is closed.
The amounts of A and B are not equal (0.40 and 0.60), showing that equilibrium does not mean equal amounts.
The reactions are still happening: A turns into B at the same rate that B turns back into A, so there is no overall change.
worked.ans: The system reached dynamic equilibrium by 10 minutes. The student is wrong because the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; only the overall concentrations stay constant.

worked.q: Sketch and explain a graph of the rate of the forward and reverse reactions against time for a reversible reaction started with reactants only.
steps: Draw the forward rate starting high at time zero and curving down.
Draw the reverse rate starting at zero and curving up.
The two lines meet at the same time and then continue as a single flat line.
Explain: forward rate falls as reactant concentration falls; reverse rate rises as product concentration rises.
Where the lines meet, rates are equal, which is the point at which dynamic equilibrium is established.
worked.ans: Forward rate decreases and reverse rate increases until they are equal; after this both stay constant and equal, showing dynamic equilibrium.

chem_edx.4.7.summary: The **Haber process** makes ammonia from **nitrogen**, extracted from the air, and **hydrogen**, obtained from natural gas: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The reaction is **reversible** and can reach a **dynamic equilibrium**, and the forward reaction is **exothermic**. The conditions used are a temperature of about **450 °C**, a pressure of about **200 atmospheres** and an **iron catalyst**, chosen as a compromise between a fast rate, a reasonable yield and acceptable cost and safety.

core.h: What the Haber process makes and why
core.p: Ammonia, NH3, is one of the most important chemicals made in industry. Most of it is used to make **nitrogen-based fertilisers** such as ammonium nitrate, which help crops grow and so help feed the world. The Haber process is the industrial method used to make it.
bullets: Product: **ammonia**, NH3, a colourless gas with a sharp smell
Main use: making **fertilisers** (e.g. ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate)
Also used to make nitric acid, explosives, dyes and cleaning products
Plants need nitrogen compounds to make proteins; they cannot use N2 from the air directly

core.p: Nitrogen and hydrogen react together to form ammonia. The reaction is **reversible**, so ammonia also breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen at the same time.
bullets: Word equation: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia
Balanced equation: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)
Ratio: **1 molecule N2 : 3 molecules H2 : 2 molecules NH3**
4 molecules of gas on the left, 2 molecules of gas on the right
The forward reaction is **exothermic** (gives out heat); the reverse reaction is **endothermic**

callouts.p: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. The reversible arrow is needed for the mark.

core.h: Where the raw materials come from
core.p: The spec requires you to know the source of each raw material. **Nitrogen is extracted from the air**, which is about 78% nitrogen. **Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas** (methane), which is reacted with steam.
bullets: Nitrogen: from **air** (separated by fractional distillation of liquid air)
Hydrogen: from **natural gas** (methane, CH4) reacted with steam
Hydrogen production also forms carbon dioxide, so the process has an environmental cost
The gases are mixed in a **1 : 3** ratio of N2 : H2, matching the equation

callouts.t: Hydrogen is not from water here
callouts.p: Edexcel mark schemes want hydrogen from natural gas (methane). 'From water' or 'from the air' does not score.

core.h: A reversible reaction that reaches dynamic equilibrium
core.p: Because the reaction is reversible, if nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia were left together in a closed system they would reach a **dynamic equilibrium**. The forward reaction (making ammonia) and the reverse reaction (ammonia decomposing) would happen at the same rate, so the concentrations of all three gases would stay constant.
bullets: At equilibrium the mixture contains N2, H2 and NH3 together
Rate of forming NH3 = rate of NH3 breaking down
Concentrations constant, not equal
Only part of the nitrogen and hydrogen is converted into ammonia: under the conditions used, about **15%** of the gases are converted on each pass through the reactor
The yield is improved overall by removing ammonia and recycling unreacted gases

callouts.p: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

core.p: The industrial plant is designed so that as much of the nitrogen and hydrogen as possible ends up as ammonia, even though each pass through the reactor converts only a small fraction.
bullets: 1. Nitrogen (from air) and hydrogen (from natural gas) are mixed in a 1 : 3 ratio
2. The gas mixture is **compressed** to about **200 atmospheres**
3. The gases pass over an **iron catalyst** at about **450 °C** in the reactor
4. Some of the nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia
5. The mixture is **cooled** in a condenser: ammonia has a much higher boiling point than N2 and H2, so it **liquefies** and is removed
6. Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are **recycled** back into the reactor, so they are not wasted

callouts.p: Ammonia boils at about -33 °C, much higher than nitrogen and hydrogen, so on cooling only ammonia condenses to a liquid while N2 and H2 stay as gases.

core.p: The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so a **low temperature** would give a **higher equilibrium yield** of ammonia. But at low temperature the **rate** is far too slow, and the iron catalyst does not work well. A **high temperature** gives a fast rate but a **low yield**. 450 °C is a **compromise temperature**.
bullets: Lower temperature: equilibrium shifts towards ammonia (the exothermic direction), so **higher yield**
Lower temperature: particles have less energy, fewer collisions have the activation energy, so **slower rate**
Higher temperature: **faster rate**, but equilibrium shifts towards N2 and H2, so **lower yield**
450 °C gives a **reasonable yield in a reasonable time**
A fast rate matters because a factory needs to make a lot of product every day

callouts.p: 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield: lower would give more ammonia but too slowly; higher would be faster but give too little ammonia.

core.p: There are **4 molecules of gas** on the left of the equation and only **2** on the right. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with **fewer gas molecules**, which is the ammonia side, so a **high pressure gives a higher yield**. High pressure also **increases the rate**, because the gas molecules are closer together and collide more often.
bullets: Higher pressure: **higher yield** (equilibrium shifts right, to fewer gas molecules)
Higher pressure: **faster rate** (more frequent collisions)
So why not use an even higher pressure? Very high pressures are **expensive**: strong, thick-walled pipes and vessels are needed and compressing gas uses a lot of energy
Very high pressures are also more **dangerous** (risk of explosion or leaks)
200 atm is a **compromise between yield, rate, cost and safety**

callouts.t: Pressure is limited by cost and safety, not yield
callouts.p: Higher pressure always helps both yield and rate here. The limit is cost of equipment and energy, and safety.

core.p: An **iron catalyst** is used to **increase the rate of reaction**. It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a **lower activation energy**, so more collisions are successful. This means a reasonable rate can be reached at a lower temperature than would otherwise be needed.
bullets: Catalyst: **iron**
Increases the rate of **both** the forward and the reverse reactions equally
So equilibrium is **reached faster**
It does **not** change the **yield** (the position of equilibrium)
It is not used up, so it can be used again and again, saving money
It allows a lower operating temperature, saving energy and fuel costs

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

core.p: Learn the three conditions as a set and be ready to explain each one in terms of both rate and yield.
bullets: Temperature: **450 °C**
Pressure: **200 atmospheres (atm)**
Catalyst: **iron**
Ammonia removed by **cooling** (liquefied); unreacted gases **recycled**

head: Condition
Value
Effect on rate
Effect on yield
Why not more extreme?
rows: Lower T too slow; higher T yield too low
Higher P = higher yield (4 to 2 gas molecules)
Higher P too expensive and dangerous

callouts.p: Write 200 atmospheres or 200 atm and 450 °C. Do not mix up the numbers: temperature 450, pressure 200.

core.p: The reaction mixture leaving the reactor contains only a small proportion of ammonia. Rather than waste the rest, the plant **separates** the ammonia by cooling and **recycles** the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen. This means that, overall, almost all of the raw materials eventually become ammonia.
bullets: Cooling liquefies ammonia, which is run off and stored
Nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases and are pumped back to the reactor
Recycling saves raw materials and money
Because ammonia is continuously removed, the system in the plant does not actually sit at equilibrium

core.p: Industrial chemists are not just looking for the highest yield. They need the **greatest amount of product per day at the lowest cost**, safely. This is why compromise conditions are chosen.
bullets: **Yield**: how much product is made compared with the maximum possible
**Rate**: how quickly the product is made
A high yield made very slowly is not useful to a factory
Energy costs: high temperatures and high pressures both need energy, often from burning fossil fuels
Equipment costs: high pressure needs stronger, more expensive plant
Safety: higher pressure increases the risk of dangerous leaks or explosions

core.h: Exam technique for Haber process questions
core.p: Haber questions are common for 4 or 6 marks. Examiners want each condition linked to its effect on **rate** AND on **yield**, with a reason, then a conclusion about compromise.
bullets: State the condition with its value and unit
Say what happens to the yield and why (exothermic forward reaction; 4 gas molecules to 2)
Say what happens to the rate and why (energy of particles; frequency of collisions)
Say why a more extreme value is not used (too slow, too costly, too dangerous)
Use the word **compromise** where it fits

callouts.t: Do not say a catalyst increases yield
callouts.p: The iron catalyst only increases the rate. It has no effect on the position of equilibrium or the yield.

analogy.p: A chef could cook a stew very slowly on a low heat and get the best possible flavour (high yield), but customers would wait all day. On a very high heat it cooks fast but much of it burns (low yield). So the chef picks a medium heat that gives good food fast enough: that is the 450 °C compromise. A pressure cooker makes food cook faster and better, but a giant, super-strong one would be very expensive and risky, so the chef uses a sensible size: that is 200 atmospheres. A good sharp knife (the catalyst) makes the work quicker but does not change how much stew you end up with. Where it breaks down: in a real reaction the lost yield is not destroyed like burnt food; ammonia simply breaks back down into nitrogen and hydrogen, which can be recycled.

terms.d: The industrial process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst at about 450 °C and 200 atm.
NH3, a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, mainly used to make fertilisers.

The amount of product obtained, often expressed as a percentage of the maximum possible.

exam.tip: Mention both yield and rate.

exam.q: Explain why a pressure higher than 200 atmospheres is not used, even though it would increase the yield.
model: Higher pressure is very expensive (stronger equipment / more energy to compress).
Higher pressure is more dangerous / greater safety risk.
exam.tip: Cost and safety, one mark each.

exam.q: Explain why increasing the pressure increases the yield of ammonia.
model: There are fewer molecules of gas on the right / 4 molecules of gas form 2.
Increasing pressure shifts the position of equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules / to the right.
exam.tip: Quote the numbers 4 and 2.

exam.q: Explain how the conditions used in the Haber process are chosen to produce ammonia economically. Refer to rate and yield in your answer.
model: Forward reaction is exothermic so a low temperature gives a high yield.
But a low temperature gives a slow rate, so 450 °C is a compromise.
4 gas molecules become 2, so high pressure gives a high yield.
High pressure also increases rate (more frequent collisions).
But very high pressure is expensive and dangerous, so 200 atm is used.
Iron catalyst increases rate without affecting yield; ammonia removed by cooling and unreacted gases recycled, so little is wasted.
exam.tip: Structure: temperature, pressure, catalyst, recycling; rate and yield for each.

worked.q: The Haber process mixes nitrogen and hydrogen in the ratio given by the equation. How many molecules of hydrogen react with 50 molecules of nitrogen, and how many molecules of ammonia could form at most?
steps: Equation: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
Ratio N2 : H2 : NH3 = 1 : 3 : 2.
Hydrogen needed: 50 × 3 = 150 molecules.
Maximum ammonia: 50 × 2 = 100 molecules.
In practice far fewer than 100 form in one pass, because the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium.
worked.ans: 150 molecules of H2 react; at most 100 molecules of NH3 could form (fewer in reality because the reaction is reversible).

worked.q: In one pass through the reactor, 15% of the nitrogen fed in is converted to ammonia. 200 tonnes of nitrogen are fed in. What mass of nitrogen is converted, and what happens to the rest?
steps: Mass converted = 15% of 200 tonnes.
15 ÷ 100 × 200 = 30 tonnes of nitrogen converted.
Unreacted nitrogen = 200 - 30 = 170 tonnes.
The unreacted nitrogen (and hydrogen) is separated from the liquefied ammonia and recycled back into the reactor.
Over many passes almost all of the nitrogen is eventually converted.
worked.ans: 30 tonnes converted in one pass; the other 170 tonnes are recycled, not wasted.

worked.q: A company suggests running the Haber process at 250 °C and 1000 atm. Evaluate this suggestion.
steps: 250 °C is lower than 450 °C: the yield would be higher because the forward reaction is exothermic.
But the rate would be much slower and the iron catalyst less effective, so less ammonia would be made per day.
1000 atm is much higher than 200 atm: the yield and rate would both increase (4 gas molecules to 2; more collisions).
But equipment able to withstand 1000 atm would be very expensive and compressing the gas would need a lot of energy.
The risk of explosion or leaks would be greater.
Conclusion: the extra yield does not justify the slow rate, extra cost and danger.
worked.ans: Not a good idea: higher yield but too slow, too expensive and too dangerous; 450 °C and 200 atm are a better compromise.

chem_edx.4.8.summary: When a system at **dynamic equilibrium** is disturbed by changing the **temperature**, **pressure** or **concentration**, the **position of equilibrium shifts** to oppose (counteract) the change. Raising the temperature favours the **endothermic** direction, raising the pressure favours the side with **fewer molecules of gas**, and adding more of a substance makes the equilibrium shift to use it up. You must be able to **predict** the direction of the shift and say what happens to the amount of product, while remembering that a **catalyst does not change** the position of equilibrium.

core.p: The **position of equilibrium** describes how much of the reactants and products are present when a reversible reaction is at dynamic equilibrium. If there are more products, the equilibrium **lies to the right**; if there are more reactants, it **lies to the left**. Changing conditions can **shift** this position.
bullets: Shift to the **right**: more products form, the forward reaction is favoured, yield of product **increases**
Shift to the **left**: more reactants form, the reverse reaction is favoured, yield of product **decreases**
After a shift, a **new equilibrium** is set up where rates are again equal
Conditions that shift equilibrium: **temperature, pressure (gases only), concentration**
A **catalyst** does **not** shift the position of equilibrium

callouts.p: The relative amounts of reactants and products in an equilibrium mixture.

core.h: The big rule: equilibrium opposes the change
core.p: There is one idea behind every prediction: **if a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes (counteracts) the change**. This idea is called **Le Chatelier's principle**. Think of the system as trying to undo whatever you did to it.
bullets: Make it hotter: the system shifts to **take in heat** (endothermic direction)
Make it colder: the system shifts to **give out heat** (exothermic direction)
Squash it (higher pressure): the system shifts to **reduce the number of gas molecules**
Add a substance: the system shifts to **use up** that substance
Remove a substance: the system shifts to **make more** of that substance

callouts.p: The position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change made to the conditions.
The system only partly reverses the change. If you heat it, the new equilibrium is still hotter than before, just with a different mixture.

core.p: In a reversible reaction, one direction is **exothermic** and the other is **endothermic**, with the same amount of energy transferred. Changing the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards one direction depending on which way is endothermic.
bullets: **Increase temperature**: equilibrium shifts in the **endothermic** direction (to take in the extra heat)
**Decrease temperature**: equilibrium shifts in the **exothermic** direction (to release heat)
If the **forward reaction is exothermic**, raising temperature shifts equilibrium **left**: less product
If the **forward reaction is endothermic**, raising temperature shifts equilibrium **right**: more product
Changing the temperature also changes the rate: a higher temperature makes equilibrium be reached faster, whichever way it shifts

callouts.p: Questions tell you if the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, often as a ΔH value. Negative ΔH means exothermic forward.

core.h: Temperature example: nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide
core.p: Brown nitrogen dioxide gas forms an equilibrium with colourless dinitrogen tetroxide: 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g). The **forward reaction is exothermic**. Because the two gases have different colours, you can **see** the equilibrium shift.
bullets: 2NO2 (brown) ⇌ N2O4 (colourless); forward reaction exothermic
**Heat** the sealed tube: equilibrium shifts **left** (endothermic direction), more NO2 forms, colour becomes **darker brown**
**Cool** the sealed tube in ice: equilibrium shifts **right** (exothermic direction), more N2O4 forms, colour becomes **paler**
The tube must be **sealed** (closed system) so the gases cannot escape
Nitrogen dioxide is toxic, so this is usually a demonstration

core.p: Pressure only affects equilibria that involve **gases**. Gas pressure is caused by gas molecules hitting the walls of the container, so **more gas molecules means more pressure**. To predict the effect, **count the molecules of gas on each side** of the balanced equation (use the numbers in front of the formulae).
bullets: **Increase pressure**: equilibrium shifts to the side with **fewer molecules of gas** (this reduces the pressure)
**Decrease pressure**: equilibrium shifts to the side with **more molecules of gas**
If both sides have the **same number** of gas molecules, changing pressure has **no effect** on the position of equilibrium
Only count **gases** (g); ignore solids and liquids when counting
Example: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) has 2 gas molecules on each side, so pressure has no effect on position

callouts.p: Write 'there are 4 molecules of gas on the left and 2 on the right' before giving the direction. It often earns a mark by itself.

core.p: In N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) there are **4 molecules of gas on the left** and **2 on the right**. So increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the **right**, increasing the yield of ammonia. That is why a high pressure (about 200 atm) is used.
bullets: Count: 1 + 3 = 4 gas molecules on the left; 2 on the right
Increase pressure: shifts right, **more ammonia**
Decrease pressure: shifts left, ammonia decomposes, **less ammonia**
Another example: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) has 3 gas molecules on the left, 2 on the right, so high pressure favours SO3

core.p: Changing the concentration of one substance in the equilibrium mixture makes the system shift to **reduce the effect** of that change. Adding more of something means the equilibrium shifts to **use it up**; removing something means the equilibrium shifts to **replace it**.
bullets: **Increase concentration of a reactant**: equilibrium shifts **right**, more products form
**Decrease concentration of a reactant**: equilibrium shifts **left**
**Increase concentration of a product**: equilibrium shifts **left**, more reactants form
**Remove a product**: equilibrium shifts **right**, more product is made to replace it
This is why industry often **removes the product** as it forms, to keep pulling the equilibrium to the right
