core.p: In the Haber process, ammonia is **removed** by cooling and liquefying it. Removing the product lowers its concentration, so the equilibrium would shift to the right to make more ammonia. In a sealed system, adding more nitrogen or hydrogen would also shift the equilibrium to the right.
bullets: Add more N2 or H2: shifts right, more NH3
Remove NH3: shifts right, more NH3 made from N2 and H2
Add more NH3: shifts left, some NH3 breaks down into N2 and H2
In a solution equilibrium, adding more of one dissolved substance shifts the equilibrium away from it; any colour change shows the shift

callouts.t: Concentration does not change which side is 'favoured' forever
callouts.p: After the shift, the system reaches a new dynamic equilibrium where forward and reverse rates are again equal.

core.h: What does NOT change the position: catalysts
core.p: A **catalyst** increases the rate of the forward and reverse reactions **by the same amount**. So it makes equilibrium be **reached faster**, but it **does not change the position of equilibrium** or the yield.
bullets: Catalyst: **no effect** on position of equilibrium
Catalyst: **no effect** on the equilibrium yield
Catalyst: equilibrium is **reached sooner**
Adding an unreactive gas or a substance not in the equation also does not take part in the equilibrium

callouts.p: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium.

core.h: Rate versus position: do not confuse them
core.p: Students often mix up two separate questions: **how fast** equilibrium is reached (rate) and **where** the equilibrium lies (position). Temperature and pressure affect both, but in different ways.
bullets: Higher temperature **always increases the rate** of both reactions
But higher temperature may increase or decrease the yield, depending on which direction is endothermic
Higher gas pressure **increases the rate** (more frequent collisions)
Higher pressure increases the yield only if the products side has **fewer** gas molecules
A catalyst changes rate only, never position

head: Change
Effect on rate
Effect on position
rows: Shifts to side with fewer gas molecules

core.p: Use the same routine every time and you will pick up the method marks even in unfamiliar reactions.
bullets: Step 1: Identify the change (temperature, pressure or concentration) and whether it is an increase or a decrease
Step 2: State how the system opposes it (take in heat, reduce gas molecules, use up the substance)
Step 3: Use the data: is the forward reaction exo or endothermic? How many gas molecules on each side? Which substance was added?
Step 4: State the direction: shifts **left** or **right**
Step 5: State the consequence: more or less product, any colour change

callouts.p: 'Shifts right' alone often gets only 1 of 2 marks. Add 'because the forward reaction is endothermic' or 'because there are fewer gas molecules on the right'.

core.p: Industrial chemists use these rules to choose conditions, but they also have to think about **rate, cost and safety**. The best conditions for yield are not always used, so a **compromise** is chosen.
bullets: Exothermic forward reaction: low temperature gives the best yield, but the rate would be too slow
Fewer gas molecules on the right: high pressure gives the best yield, but very high pressure is expensive and dangerous
Removing product and recycling unreacted reactants keeps the overall conversion high
Haber process compromise: 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst

analogy.p: Picture a see-saw with reactants on the left and products on the right, carefully balanced. If you push down on one end (add more reactant), the see-saw responds by tipping the extra weight across, moving material to the other side until it balances again. A system at equilibrium behaves like a stubborn friend who always does the opposite of what you do: turn the heating up and they open the window (take in heat); squeeze them into a smaller room and they stand closer together in fewer groups (fewer gas molecules). Where it breaks down: a see-saw rebalances by moving one object, but an equilibrium rebalances by changing the rates of reactions until they are equal again, and it never fully undoes the change you made.

terms.d: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
The relative amounts of reactants and products in the equilibrium mixture.
The position of equilibrium moves towards the products: more product forms.
The position of equilibrium moves towards the reactants: more reactant forms.
If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings (ΔH negative).
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings (ΔH positive).
The reaction from left to right in the equation.
The reaction from right to left in the equation.
Caused by gas molecules colliding with the container walls; more gas molecules in the same volume gives higher pressure.
The amount of a substance in a given volume of solution or gas mixture.
The amount of product obtained; a shift to the right increases the equilibrium yield.
Speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally; does not change the position of equilibrium.
A system where no substances can enter or leave, needed for equilibrium.
Conditions chosen to balance yield against rate, cost and safety.

mistakes.w: Increasing the temperature shifts equilibrium to the right.
mistakes.r: Increasing the temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which may be left or right depending on the reaction.

mistakes.w: Increasing the pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with more molecules.
mistakes.r: Increasing the pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer molecules of gas.

mistakes.w: Counting all substances, including solids and liquids, when predicting the effect of pressure.
mistakes.r: Only count the molecules of gas on each side, using the balancing numbers.

mistakes.w: A catalyst shifts the equilibrium to the right / increases yield.
mistakes.r: A catalyst has no effect on the position of equilibrium; it only makes equilibrium be reached faster.

mistakes.w: Pressure always affects equilibrium.
mistakes.r: Pressure has no effect on position if both sides have the same number of gas molecules, or if no gases are involved.

mistakes.w: Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium to the left.
mistakes.r: Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, to use up the added reactant and make more product.

mistakes.w: The equilibrium shifts to make the reaction faster.
mistakes.r: The equilibrium shifts to oppose the change; rate and position are separate ideas.

mistakes.w: Raising the temperature favours the exothermic reaction because it gives out heat.
mistakes.r: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reaction, which takes in the extra heat.

mistakes.w: Heating 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 makes the mixture paler.
mistakes.r: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts equilibrium left, making more brown NO2: the mixture gets darker.

exam.q: State the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium.
model: No effect / position stays the same.
exam.tip: Rate changes, position does not.

exam.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), predict the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield of ammonia. Explain your answer.
model: Yield of ammonia increases / equilibrium shifts right.
Because there are fewer gas molecules on the right (2) than the left (4).
exam.tip: Quote the molecule numbers.

exam.q: The reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g) has an exothermic forward reaction. State the effect on the amount of C if the temperature is increased.
model: Amount of C decreases / equilibrium shifts left.
Because the reverse reaction is endothermic (and is favoured by increased temperature).
exam.tip: Identify the endothermic direction first.

exam.q: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Explain why changing the pressure does not change the position of this equilibrium.
model: There are the same number of gas molecules on each side (2 and 2).
So neither direction reduces the number of gas molecules / pressure has no effect on position.
exam.tip: Count both sides.

exam.q: 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g). NO2 is brown and N2O4 is colourless. The forward reaction is exothermic. Describe and explain what you would see when a sealed tube of the mixture is put into hot water.
model: The colour becomes darker brown.
The equilibrium shifts to the left.
Because the reverse reaction is endothermic / increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction.
exam.tip: Observation, direction, reason.

exam.q: For the same NO2 / N2O4 equilibrium, predict what happens to the colour when the pressure is increased (ignore the effect of squashing on the colour). Explain your answer.
model: Equilibrium shifts to the right.
Because there are fewer gas molecules on the right (1 compared with 2).
So more colourless N2O4 forms and the mixture becomes paler.
exam.tip: Link molecule count to direction, then direction to colour.

exam.q: In a reversible reaction in solution, extra reactant is added. State and explain the effect on the concentration of the product.
model: Concentration of product increases.
Because the equilibrium shifts to the right to use up the added reactant / oppose the change.
exam.tip: Use 'oppose the change'.

exam.q: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Predict the conditions of temperature and pressure that would give the highest equilibrium yield of SO3. Explain your answer.
model: Low temperature.
Because the forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering temperature shifts equilibrium right.
High pressure.
Because there are fewer gas molecules on the right (2) than on the left (3).
exam.tip: One mark for each condition, one for each reason.

exam.q: Explain why removing ammonia from the reaction mixture increases the amount of ammonia made in the Haber process.
model: Removing ammonia lowers its concentration.
So the equilibrium shifts to the right to produce more ammonia / to oppose the change.
exam.tip: Mention the shift direction explicitly.

exam.q: A reversible reaction is: X(g) + Y(g) ⇌ 2Z(g), forward reaction endothermic. Evaluate how changing temperature, pressure and the concentration of X would affect the yield of Z, and suggest the best conditions for a high yield.
model: Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium right (forward is endothermic), so yield of Z increases.
Decreasing temperature would shift equilibrium left and decrease yield of Z.
There are 2 gas molecules on each side, so changing pressure has no effect on the yield.
Increasing concentration of X shifts equilibrium right, increasing yield of Z.
Removing Z as it forms would also shift equilibrium right.
Best: high temperature, high concentration of X (pressure chosen for rate / cost, not yield); a catalyst would not change yield but would increase rate.
exam.tip: Treat each variable separately, then conclude.

worked.q: Predict the effect of (a) increasing the temperature and (b) decreasing the pressure on the yield of ammonia in N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), where the forward reaction is exothermic.
steps: (a) Increasing temperature: the system opposes the change by taking in heat.
The endothermic direction is the reverse reaction (because the forward is exothermic).
So the equilibrium shifts left and the yield of ammonia decreases.
(b) Count gas molecules: 1 + 3 = 4 on the left, 2 on the right.
Decreasing pressure: the system opposes the change by making more gas molecules.
The side with more gas molecules is the left, so equilibrium shifts left and yield of ammonia decreases.
worked.ans: (a) Yield of ammonia decreases (shift left, to the endothermic side). (b) Yield of ammonia decreases (shift left, to the side with more gas molecules).

worked.q: CO(g) + 2H2(g) ⇌ CH3OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. A student wants to increase the equilibrium yield of methanol. Give three changes that would do this and explain each.
steps: Count gas molecules: 1 + 2 = 3 on the left, 1 on the right.
Change 1: increase pressure, because equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules (right).
Change 2: decrease temperature, because the forward reaction is exothermic so a lower temperature shifts equilibrium right.
Change 3: increase the concentration of CO or H2 (or remove methanol), because equilibrium shifts right to use up the extra reactant / replace the product.
Note: adding a catalyst would not change the yield, only the rate.
worked.ans: Increase pressure, lower temperature, add more CO or H2 (or remove CH3OH); each shifts equilibrium to the right.

worked.q: A sealed flask contains an equilibrium of colourless N2O4 and brown NO2: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g). The forward reaction is endothermic. The flask is placed in ice. Predict and explain the colour change.
steps: Placing in ice decreases the temperature.
The system opposes this by shifting in the exothermic direction.
Forward reaction is endothermic, so the reverse (making N2O4) is exothermic.
Equilibrium shifts to the left, so more colourless N2O4 forms.
Less brown NO2 remains.
worked.ans: The mixture becomes paler (less brown) because the equilibrium shifts left, in the exothermic direction, forming more colourless N2O4.
